articles.title: Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles
articles.summary: Three months after leaving Lopez Inc., Gabby Lopez’s new game plan is clear

blocks.text: Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it

When Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III sold his family’s shares in the main Lopez holding company in August, he said the move would allow his family to “channel our family’s resources into businesses aligned with our personal mission,” adding that more announcements would come in due time.
Three months later, his new game plan is clear. It centers on two companies that serve everyday Filipinos: ABS-CBN and Rockwell Land.

On Thursday, November 12, First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH), led by Gabby’s cousin, Federico “Piki” Lopez, agreed to sell its 90.74% voting stake in Rockwell Land. The buyer is Gabby’s and his siblings’ private firm, Crème Investment Corporation, and the price tag is P15.92 billion.

This completes a 94-day asset swap that began on August 10. Back then, Crème sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. to San Miguel boss Ramon S. Ang for about P11 billion. Lopez Inc. was originally built as the untouchable top holding company meant to protect the family empire from outside takeovers. (READ: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN)

blocks.caption: THEN…The Rockwell property with  the old Meralco power plant (upper right) in Makati City. Rappler/Rockwell brand rap file image

blocks.text: For decades, Rockwell Land has been the Lopez Group’s luxury lifestyle and consumer jewel. Started in 1995 on the site of an old Meralco power plant in Makati, Rockwell turned an industrial lot into Rockwell Center, which is now home to Power Plant Mall, high-end condos, serviced apartments, and offices.

blocks.caption: …AND NOW. Bird’s eye view of Rockwell Makati with Power Plant Mall at the center. Courtesy of Rockwell Land

blocks.text: This focus on everyday consumers is a natural fit for Gabby who spent his career in TV, entertainment, and public-facing brands. Just two days after the August sale, Gabby and his cousins pledged P2.2 billion of their own money to help rebuild ABS-CBN. He explained why: “ABS-CBN has been part of this family for generations. The mission our family set out to pursue remains the heartbeat of this family—to be in the service of the Filipino. We are putting our own money behind this conviction.” (READ: Gabby Lopez: Man on a mission)

This is a sharp contrast from Piki Lopez’s world at FPH and First Gen, an ascetic, heavy-infrastructure universe of geothermal steam fields, gas turbines, and pumped-storage hydropower projects that require tens of billions of pesos and years, sometimes decades, of engineering before they make money. At the 2026 annual stockholders’ meetings of FPH and First Gen, Piki repeatedly framed his leadership around the “compounding” value of long-term choices, and that “direction over speed” matters more. In other words, a slow-and-steady approach built for power grids rather than quick profits.
Gabby does not seem to be retreating from the family business. Instead, he is separating the group’s lifestyle and media brands from FPH’s power business and bringing them under his own control.

blocks.caption: BOSS. Ambassador Manuel “Manolo” Lopez speaks at a corporate event following Rockwell Land Corp.’s listing on May 12, 2012, in Rockwell Power Plant Mall’s premises in Makati City. Courtesy of Rockwell Land FB

blocks.text: Rockwell also has deep ties to Gabby’s late uncle, Manuel “Manolo” Lopez. Manolo ran Meralco for over 30 years and was deeply disappointed when the family and business group, both led then by his older brother Oscar, the father of Piki, forced FPH to let go of Meralco in 2009 to pay off First Gen’s geothermal debts. Manolo was quoted then saying, “Meralco would have been my parents’ legacy.” In March and April 2026, Manolo’s children joined Gabby and other cousins in publicly challenging Piki’s leadership. Buying Rockwell brings a business closely linked to Manolo’s side of the family under Crème’s direct control.
Beyond family history and culture, this deal solves a major money problem for Gabby’s branch: ABS-CBN needs cash, and Rockwell makes it.

In 2025, Rockwell earned P4.73 billion. ABS-CBN lost P4.72 billion. Crème has already pledged P766.7 million to ABS-CBN’s P6-billion fundraising drive. Buying Rockwell gives Gabby’s family an established, profitable company that brings in its own money. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

blocks.caption: CASH COW. Rockwell Land’s 2025 earnings. Courtesy of Rockwell Land website

blocks.text: Before losing its broadcast franchise in 2020, ABS-CBN was a reliable cash machine for its parent firm, Lopez Holdings, former Benpres Holdings and one level below Lopez Inc in the Lopez group shareholder tree. ABS-CBN paid Lopez Holdings P447 million in dividends in 2018 and P269 million in 2019. Once the network went off the air, those payouts vanished. From 2020 to 2025, ABS-CBN racked up about P45.5 billion in losses. (READ: ABS-CBN is now 84% content — and still losing money. Can P6 billion fix it?)

With ABS-CBN out of cash, Lopez Holdings had to lean almost completely on FPH, which owns the group’s power and property businesses. From 2021 to 2025, FPH paid Lopez Holdings a flat P567 million a year in dividends. After Lopez Holdings paid its bills and shared profits with public stockholders, only about P247 million actually reached Lopez, Inc. in 2025.

FPH’s own financial records show where that money came from. In 2025, subsidiary Rockwell paid FPH roughly P630 million in dividends. Meralco—where FPH still owns a 3.95% stake—paid another P1.115 billion. Together, those two companies gave FPH P1.75 billion in cash dividends. That is more than triple the P567 million FPH sent up to Lopez Holdings.

FPH didn’t just hoard the extra cash. As a public company, it had debts, operating costs, outside shareholders, and massive power projects to pay for. First Gen and its subsidiary, Energy Development Corporation, were pouring money into geothermal drilling, hydropower, and battery storage while paying off loans. First Gen President and COO Giles Puno noted at this year’s annual meeting that while the company aims to pay out 30% of its yearly recurring profit, those payouts depend on spending needs, growth plans, and debt payments. To save cash, First Gen cut how much it paid as yearly dividend to its parent FPH from P0.90 per share in 2024 to P0.80 in 2025.

So most of the Piki-led power group’s profits stayed locked inside the operating companies. For family members at the very top of the corporate ladder, including Gabby and the heirs of Manolo, that meant waiting years for bigger payouts. Buying Rockwell lets Crème skip all those corporate middlemen. Instead of waiting for cash to trickle up through FPH, Lopez Holdings, and Lopez, Inc., Gabby’s firm can soon collect dividends straight from the source as Rockwell’s main owner.

blocks.caption: The company the Lopezes gave up Meralco for: EDC, from oil crisis child to takeover target

blocks.text: Rockwell’s net profit for parent shareholders climbed from P3.11 billion in 2023 to P3.71 billion in 2024, reaching P4.73 billion in 2025. The 2025 number got a boost from a one-time gain after buying Alabang Commercial Corporation. Even without that extra boost, Rockwell still earned about P4.1 billion.

Its cash flow has grown right along with its profits. Rockwell brought in P2 billion in cash from daily operations in 2025, up sharply from P144 million in 2024, even though real estate requires heavy upfront spending on land and construction. Its regular dividends grew steadily too, rising from P0.0752 per share in 2023 to P0.1018 in 2024, and hitting P0.1212 in 2025. Renting out commercial spaces gives Rockwell a steady safety net beyond just selling condos. Power Plant Mall in Makati, its office buildings, and its December 2025 purchase of Alabang Commercial Corporation—which added Alabang Town Center and a nearby office tower—bring in reliable rental cash.

blocks.caption: Refreshed Alabang Town Center? What shoppers can expect now that Rockwell has near-full control.

blocks.text: Of course, Rockwell has big bills of its own. Its P21.6-billion Alabang deal is being paid in installments through December 2027, and it raised P10 billion in retail bonds in March 2026 to fund active projects. It can’t pay dividend to its owners every single peso it makes. Still, it gives Gabby a healthy business that makes money rather than drains it.
Rockwell and ABS-CBN share more than just the Lopez family name. Over the last four years, Rockwell has been one of the main buyers of the real estate ABS-CBN sold to raise cash.

In 2022, Rockwell bought properties from ABS-CBN for P786 million, followed by another P733 million deal in 2023. Those sales gave the network profit gains of P246 million and P232 million. In 2024, Rockwell bought more ABS-CBN land for about P679 million—booking a P223.1-million gain for the broadcaster—and agreed to buy ABS-CBN’s Iloilo property for P91.4 million. Later company filings showed even more property deals between the two firms.

Their shared history goes back even further. Before Rockwell went public in 2012, its housing arm built the 53 Benitez condos in Quezon City on the site of an old movie studio. Lopez Holdings, then known as Benpres Holdings, also owned 24.5% of Rockwell directly before selling it to FPH in August 2009.

Smaller day-to-day ties are still in place. ABS-CBN Holdings Corporation, which handles the network’s depository receipts, keeps its main office at Rockwell Business Center Sheridan in Mandaluyong. Lopez Holdings also pays office rent to Rockwell.

No merger or money-sharing plan between Rockwell and ABS-CBN has been announced, and they remain completely separate companies. Still, Rockwell has repeatedly stepped in to buy the properties ABS-CBN needed to sell, and now Gabby is taking over Rockwell itself.
Until August, Crème’s 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. gave Gabby’s family a small, indirect piece of several businesses, but very little control over dividend payouts.

Under the P15.92-billion deal approved by FPH on November 12, Crème will buy 86.58% of Rockwell’s common shares, plus voting preferred shares that raise its total voting power to 90.74%. Once regulators approve the deal and Crème makes a required buyout offer to the remaining public stockholders, it becomes the controlling owner. That gives Crème a direct say over Rockwell’s board and dividend payouts, within the limits of corporate law, loan rules, and minority shareholder rights.

If Rockwell keeps paying its 2025 dividend rate of P0.1212 per share, Crème’s incoming block of 5.30 billion common shares would bring in about P642 million a year before taxes. Future payouts aren’t guaranteed—they will depend on Rockwell’s profits, spending needs, and board votes.

Three months after leaving Lopez, Inc., Gabby Lopez’s new game plan is clear. He has fresh cash for ABS-CBN, the network he spent his life building, and direct control of Rockwell Land, a profitable lifestyle developer that already makes money. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Beijing faces its Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
articles.summary: China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image on…

image.caption: Although no government has officially confirmed the meeting, some media outlets have already dubbed it 'the new Yalta'Image: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen this week.

China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.

The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world?
Is the world set for a 'new Yalta'?

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.

blocks.caption: The Yalta summit saw Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill represent the three main victorious powers of WWIIImage: RIA Novosti/SNA/imago

blocks.text: At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.

In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.
The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.
End of campaign to isolate Putin?

A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.

As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
EU wary of being left out of Ukraine talks

The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.
Europe seeks role in Ukraine peace talks

"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.
She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.

For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.
"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.
Beijing and Moscow stick to 'no limits' partnership
Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.

The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.
At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.
China helping Russia from the sidelines

Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.
While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.
Russia needs China trade more than ever
Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome.

"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.

"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.
What are the actual limits of China-Russia axis?
In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.
Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.

However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.

Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.
China getting a 'privileged vantage point' on Ukraine war
But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.

MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."

"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.
Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.
"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.

articles.title: Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
articles.summary:
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine

Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit…

blocks.text: Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. Likened to the 1945 summit at Yalta, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.
Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.
“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.
“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.
“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”
German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.
“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine, and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.
“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

Zelensky has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”, invoking the conference in Crimea when the then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.
“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.
“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.
“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo. It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.
More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

articles.title: Party-list reform bill may be tackled in 2027 ahead of 2028 polls - Adiong
articles.summary: The House of Representatives may begin plenary discussions on a proposed measure reforming the party-list system next year, the chair of the House Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms said…

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 2:01pm

The House of Representatives may begin plenary discussions on a proposed measure reforming the party-list system next year, the chair of the House Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms said Sunday.
Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said Congress still has time to tackle House Bill No. 9906 before the 2028 national elections, although the pace of deliberations remains uncertain.
“Palagay ko baka ma-tackle na ito next year na,” Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.
“I think this might be tackled next year,” he said.
“Mayroon pa tayong isang taon bago tayo magkaroon ng presidential elections. Hindi lang natin sigurado kung paano yung flow ng debate,” he added.

Among the key provisions of HB 9906 is a proposed ban on individuals within the second degree of consanguinity or affinity to incumbent senators or House members from being nominated as party-list representatives.

The measure also requires party-list organizations to certify that they were not established by political dynasties and are not linked to individuals with beneficial interests in government contracts.
Adiong said a technical working group had already been formed to study the proposed measure.
He said the committee was hoping to submit its report to the plenary before the year ends to allow deliberations to begin.
“Before the end of this year, magre-report na tayo kung makasingit pa po tayo sa plenaryo ng ating committee report, nang sa ganun magsimula na po ang debate,” he said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Gymshark in trademark battle that threatens future of small fitness business
articles.summary:
Exclusive: British sportswear firm is seeking to obtain rights to The Conditioning Club, which is also the name of a Gloucestershire gym

Gymshark, the

blocks.text: Gymshark, the £1bn British sportswear firm started in a family garage, is locked in a trademark battle that threatens the future of a small fitness business.

Ben Francis, the university dropout who started sewing his own gym clothes in his parents’ garage and is now estimated to be worth £800m, is trying to add The Conditioning Club to his Gymshark stable of trademarks.
However, The Conditioning Club is also the name of a gym and fitness business based on an industrial estate in the Gloucestershire town of Fairford.
Founded by John Watson, who is the same age as 34-year-old Francis, the company registered its name at the UK Intellectual Property Office (UKIPO) for gym and fitness services five years ago.
Watson, who has nine staff and three self-employed personal trainers serving about 500 members, is now awaiting the outcome of proceedings by the UKIPO.

“When I registered our name, I thought I had done what I needed to do to protect us,” says Watson. “Five years later, we have members, employees, premises, relationships with schools and sports clubs and a genuine local community built around The Conditioning Club name.

“I never imagined that I would find myself having to defend our name, particularly against a business like Gymshark, which like us started from humble beginnings. I had previously looked to Ben and Gymshark as an example of what a small UK fitness-related business can achieve.”

blocks.caption: Customers outside Gymshark’s first retail store in Regent Street, London. The fitness and apparel firm was valued at £1bn in 2020 when US private equity firm General Atlantic bought a 21% stake. Photograph: Stephen Chung/Alamy

blocks.text: Francis founded Gymshark in 2012 and US private equity firm General Atlantic took a stake in 2020, making the company a “unicorn” with a £1.25bn valuation and Francis a multimillionaire while still in his 20s. He was the recipient of an MBE for services to the commerce and the economy at 30.
Last March, Gymshark applied to register Conditioning Club and The Conditioning Club as trademarks to offer services in classes including clothing, retail and entertainment services.

While Gymshark did not apply for a trademark covering fitness and training services, one of its applications is in the same class as Watson’s, as he had been selling branded gear for a number of years.

Watson moved to oppose the trademark application in the class he has registered to protect his brand. He also applied to extend his trademark to cover the classes, such as retail, that Gymshark had applied for that he had not thought to register when he set up his business.

Gymshark opposed him and also applied to the UKIPO to invalidate his original trademark ownership on the grounds that The Conditioning Club name is descriptive, essentially too generic and not distinct enough to be allowed to be trademarked.
after newsletter promotion
However, Gymshark has multiple trademark registrations for the equally generic “Lifting Club” brand.
Watson’s legal costs are climbing towards £30,000. He recently launched a crowdfunding campaign via CrowdJustice. It has raised just over £5,000 to help.

“It feels deeply intimidating, the financial imbalance between us is enormous,” he said. “They can afford a prolonged trademark battle. It is a very David and Goliath situation. I’m happy to agree a sensible arrangement with them. This is about something much simpler: protecting the name of the business I created and have spent the last five years building.”
A legal battle stretching to almost 18 months with a small player in the fitness industry is at odds with the ethos and brand image on which Gymshark has built its name.
Earlier this week, the company donated £10,000 to the owner of a gym and Redditch that burned down.

Other acts of generosity include donating almost £9,000 to help a British athlete raise funds to achieve his dream of getting to the Olympics, after the long jumper had been forced to get a job as a delivery driver to continue training.
Gymshark declined to comment on the trademark battle.

articles.title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary:
International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel

The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this…

blocks.text: The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”

blocks.caption: The Kutupalong Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Munir Uz Zaman/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.
This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a military airstrike on a market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, a rebel-held area in western Rakhine state, 28 September 2026. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The former general is separately b​eing investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.

For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.
The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.

The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.

blocks.caption: Min Aung Hlaing, president of Myanmar, speaks during a meeting with Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin in August. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/Pool AP/AP

blocks.text: However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.

Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.
More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.
A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.
“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

articles.title: Planned asylum seeker detention centre next to Oxfordshire sewage works criticised
articles.summary:
Thames Water says detainees at proposed accommodation should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells

A Home Office plan to build asylum seeker detention facilities next to a…

blocks.text: A Home Office plan to build asylum seeker detention facilities next to a sewage pump is facing objections after water company officials warned that detainees should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells.

Proposed secure accommodation blocks at Campsfield House immigration removal centre in Oxfordshire will be 20 metres from a sewage pumping station, according to a written submission from Thames Water.

A senior development manager at the company wrote that it could give rise to “amenity effects, including odour, noise, vibration, lighting associated with maintenance activities, insects and flies” for any inhabitants. In a previous submission, the company wrote that any development may lead to sewage flooding.
The warnings, which come as the government hopes to expand the immigration detention estate by 40%, have been seized upon by campaigners against the expansion.

Ally Swadling, the lead legal education officer at the charity Right to Remain, said: “Thames Water’s concerns about sewage infrastructure at Campsfield show how little regard is being given to even the most basic standards of sanitation and human dignity.
“They reinforce what we already know – this government is putting its political priorities above people’s lives and wellbeing.”
The centre near Kidlington re-opened in December 2025 after it was shut in 2018 following years of problems, including suicides, riots, escapes and complaints about conditions.

The Home Office is planning to increase the centre’s capacity from 160 bed spaces to 400, and to convert existing buildings. According to the Thames Water submission in October, officials also “raised concerns regarding capacity within the foul water, surface water and water supply networks” in the local area.
A separate 2015 written consultation response, which was submitted in June, states the development may lead to sewage flooding in the area.

“Thames Water request that an impact study be undertaken to ascertain, with a greater degree of certainty, whether the proposed development will lead to overloading of existing infrastructure,” it said.
Written representations, including that of Thames Water, will be heard at a public inquiry beginning on 14 December.
Oxfordshire county council has formally objected to the expansion of Campsfield House, saying it risks intensifying existing public concern, and called for the site to be shut permanently.
after newsletter promotion
According to the Home Office, nearly 80,000 people have been returned or deported from the UK since the 2024 election to the end of June 2026, an increase of 52% on the previous two years.

Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said: “Detention is a harmful, dehumanising experience that must only be used as a last resort. Evidence shows it’s ineffective, expensive and damages people forced to endure it.

“Instead of expanding sites such as Campsfield House immigration removal centre, and in this case, in a way that could potentially be detrimental to the health and wellbeing of people staying there, the government must instead use community-based alternatives detention, which have proven to be effective and much cheaper.”

A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “We are confident in our plans for Campsfield immigration removal centre and will continue to engage constructively with the Planning Inspectorate as the process moves forward. We are committed to increasing the removal of those with no right to remain in the UK. Expanding our detention capacity plays an important role in achieving this.”
Thames Water said they had nothing to add to their response.

articles.title: Could universal basic income be part of the solution in an AI economy?
articles.summary: The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists are not convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask…

image.caption: Artificial Intelligence is predicted to cost hundreds of thousands of jobs in Germany aloneImage: Tobias Schwarz/AFP

blocks.text: At the German government's 2026 "Digital Summit" in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July this year, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring last year, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
The impending job rupture

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world. This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socio-economic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."
How AI is changing the working world
Why tech bosses love UBI

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the non-profit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of UBI.

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income (UBI) is very old: The English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances that they said AI would bring. In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable.

Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

But Herrmann says it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She is not convinced that organizations like hers and people like Elon Musk want the same thing. "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."
Is AI killing creative jobs?

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea. Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at Oxford University and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy also thinks that is a good idea, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he told DW by email. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"
Work-life integration: A new ideal?

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history: Partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact: AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socio-economic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she puts it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argues, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work: "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," Herrmann said. "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

articles.title: Maria Ressa speaks at 2026 ASEAN Business and Investment Summit
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence can reproduce ‘the worst of who we are,’ says Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence can reproduce ‘the worst of who we are,’ says Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa warned that artificial intelligence deployment by the private sector has outpaced regulation and control by the government.
Ressa delivered a keynote speech and joined a fireside chat on “Trust in the Age of AI,” at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit in Parañaque City on Sunday, November 15.
She noted that because AI models scrape training material from the internet, it can reproduce “the worst of who we are.”

“It can work for you the same way social media works for content creators, but it is a Faustian bargain if you do not look at the design,” Ressa said during the fireside chat, hosted by veteran journalist Karen Davila.
The two-day business summit, happening on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, ends on Sunday. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US floated idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv would not concede territory but would put the question to a national referendum if Ukraine received security guarantees, a right to a strong military, and…

blocks.text: TALKS. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy meets with US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, on the day of the European Political Community summit, following Kushner's trip to Russia, in Dublin, Ireland, on November 12, 2026.
Cathal McNaughton/Reuters

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv would not concede territory but would put the question to a national referendum if Ukraine received security guarantees, a right to a strong military, and reconstruction funds

items: US negotiators have proposed Ukraine's potential withdrawal from Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, marking a new development in peace talks with Russia.
President Zelenskyy emphasized that Ukraine is not ready to concede territory but would consider a national referendum if provided with security guarantees and support for rebuilding.
The recent talks concluded without major breakthroughs, although a large prisoner exchange was agreed upon, and discussions about a potential energy ceasefire are ongoing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

KYIV, Ukraine – US negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine’s potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskyy said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday, November 14.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” he said.
“That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation.”
Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.

Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, November 13, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.

“We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.

US President Donald Trump‘s envoy ‌and son-in-law Jared Kushner said on Saturday that the two sides had set out “maximalist positions” in the talks this week, but in private discussions both “understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war.”
“Serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions,” Kushner said in a social media post.

Zelenskyy also dismissed Putin’s suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, saying it reflected Moscow’s inability to take the city by force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.
“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” he said.

Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelenskyy said.
Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.

The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelenskyy said.
The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.

Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskyy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.
“Putin personally does not support a ceasefire,” he said.

Zelenskyy met Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks in Moscow. He said the US negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks.
In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine’s largest financial and military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia.

At the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as EU officials.
Kushner said the US focus was now on “facilitating direct engagement between Moscow and European partners and preparing the agenda for the next round of trilateral talks.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: ASEAN hosting an 'investment' to boost PH standings - Adiong
articles.summary: The hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits is an investment to boost the country's presence, a lawmaker said on Sunday as the global meet officially started.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 12:56pm
The hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits is an investment to boost the country's presence, a lawmaker said on Sunday as the global meet officially started.

While the government's spending of P22.9 billion for the hosting has raised questions from various sectors, Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Adiong said that it's the country's duty to sustain the cooperation among the Southeast Asia region through the event.

"Tayo po ‘yung chair ng ASEAN, so kailangan na hindi natin ito balewalain. I think it's part of our obligation to build a strong community of nations, lalong lalo na itong mga kapitbahay natin, kung saan very strong ang ating bilateral economic trade. Kailangan natin sustentuhin ang ganitong klaseng kooperasyon na ito," he told Super Radyo dzBB.

(We currently chair ASEAN, so we should not take this lightly. I believe it's part of our obligation to build a strong community of nations, especially these neighbors of ours, where our bilateral economic trade is very strong. We need to sustain this kind of cooperation.)
"I think this is part of an investment for the country to boost its international standing in relation to our being part of the ASEAN corridor," he added.
Gathered in Manila, the leaders of the 11 ASEAN countries are expected to discuss the Middle East crisis, food security, and transnational crimes, among other issues.
Leaders from outside the region, including Australia, Canada, Brazil, and the US, are also present.
For his part, Adiong said the country cannot afford to compromise its hosting responsibility.

"You also have to remember na ‘yung ating mga bisita ay mga heads of states ng mga countries. You really cannot give any inch of compromise na magkaroon impossible security breach. Kailangan natin i-secure sila," he said.
(You also have to remember that our guests are heads of states of countries. You really cannot give any inch of compromise for a security breach to happen. We need to secure them.)
Ahead of the summit, the Philippines and Canada concluded negotiations for a free trade agreement (FTA), with both countries aiming to sign the pact in 2027.
Meanwhile, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva have discussed strengthening agricultural cooperation to protect local farms and support food security.
Marcos earlier said the hosting of the ASEAN summit "is an important opportunity to create more jobs, support local businesses and open new doors for our people." —RF, GMA News

articles.title: After midterm sweep, Democrats split over Trump, cost-cutting agenda
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump retains significant executive authority to block much of the Democrats' agenda, complicating the party's efforts to lower costs, the central issue voters gave Democrats…

items: Democrats are united in wanting to provide relief from high costs but are divided on how to achieve this and how to approach President Trump.
The party faces ideological tensions between moderates and progressives, with debates on whether to adopt a bolder agenda or focus on centrist policies.
There is a collective concern among party members that they must capitalize on their electoral victory to address voters' issues, or risk losing support in the future.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Fresh from a midterm election landslide, Democrats met in Denver this week united in wanting to deliver voters relief from high costs, but split over how to achieve that, what lessons to draw from their victory and how combative they should be toward President Donald Trump.

Despite the celebratory mood after the November 3 rout of Republicans, tensions between moderates and a restive progressive wing surfaced at the party’s first major gathering since its victory, along with anxiety that the party could squander the opportunity voters had handed it.

The gathering offered an early glimpse of the battle to define its future as prospective 2028 presidential candidates and senior leaders debated how to turn electoral success into a governing agenda while navigating long-standing ideological and generational divides.

The conference, hosted by Majority Democrats, a group that advocates for younger party leaders and against left-wing activism, offered a forum for the jockeying now underway as Democrats debate what lessons to draw from their midterm win and begin the search for a 2028 White House standard-bearer.

Speakers disagreed over whether to embrace a bolder progressive agenda or tack toward the center, exposing competing approaches to lowering food, healthcare and housing costs, while working alongside Trump, who retains veto power for two more years.

California Representative Ro Khanna, a progressive and potential presidential candidate, urged Democrats to stop chasing the political center and embrace a bolder agenda, including universal healthcare, a wealth tax, a $25 federal minimum wage, deep Pentagon cuts and abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

By contrast, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a moderate and another potential 2028 contender, argued the party should move beyond ideological litmus tests, saying voters “don’t give a damn” about such debates and care instead about whether Democrats can deliver results.
The breadth of the Democratic victories has allowed moderates and progressives to argue that voters have endorsed their vision for the party’s future.

“It’s to be expected that there will be a big debate because the Democratic victory was so broad it swept in centrists, southern Democrats and more progressive and left-wing Democrats,” Democratic strategist Elaine Kamarck told Reuters.

Trump retains significant executive authority to block much of the Democrats’ agenda, complicating the party’s efforts to lower costs, the central issue voters gave Democrats control of Congress to fix.

Democrats are projected to hold at least 255 seats to ​Republicans’ 169 in the US House, with 12 contests still ​undecided. In the Senate, the breakdown will be ⁠at least 55-44, with Democrats possibly gaining one more seat in Alaska when vote-counting is completed.
One of the most striking debates in Denver centered on how to govern with Trump still in the White House.
James Talarico, the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Texas since 1988, urged Democrats to work with Trump.

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” Talarico said, drawing tepid applause. “We’re tired of being pitted against each other.”
He found an ally in Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand, who said he encouraged Democrats at campaign events to applaud Republicans and that partisan warfare will not deliver results.
“The only way we’re going to fix that is by fixing it together,” Sand said.
Minutes later, US Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Eric Holder, who was attorney general in the Obama administration, largely rejected accommodation with Trump.

Raskin, expected to become chairman of the House Judiciary Committee in January and oversee investigations of Trump next year, said the Republican Party had become an authoritarian cult of personality.

“We’re going to reassert all of the powers of Congress that have been surrendered and abdicated by the MAGA Congress to King Trump,” Raskin said. “We’re going to enforce the Constitution against him.”
Holder warned Democrats against pursuing bipartisanship.

“If we retreat into caution, if we operate out of fear, if we take refuge in the niceties of the old Washington and seek approval from those who have been and are actively dismantling our institutions, we will fail.”
There has been a long-simmering debate inside the party over whether to move further left or pursue a more centrist agenda, and this election has only intensified those tensions.
Almost everyone who spoke at the conference agreed the party’s top priority was lowering costs and improving life for working families.

It was a theme echoed by New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries, set to become US House Speaker, and several prospective 2028 presidential candidates, including Shapiro, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and Khanna.
But splits emerged over how to achieve that.
Jeffries, a moderate, was heckled by a group of protesters, who accused him of being too timid to deliver change and called for a House leader who embraced a more populist progressive agenda.

Khanna and Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, another progressive who this week challenged more centrist Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for the party’s top leadership job in the Senate, called for populist, government-funded economic solutions.
There was a collective anxiety among the speakers that the party might squander one of the biggest victories it has achieved in a generation.
Many speakers described the win not as an enduring mandate, but rather a temporary opportunity voters had given them to fix the country’s problems.
Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego, another potential presidential contender, noted that many Hispanic voters who voted for Trump in 2024 backed Democrats this month.
“It was not, though, a love letter to the Democratic Party,” Gallego said. “It is a short-term loan that we need to keep paying, or we will lose it.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.summary:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings

The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this…

blocks.text: The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.

The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.

Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

blocks.caption: Protesters in Manila on Friday object to Donald Trump’s participation in the Asean summit. Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPA

blocks.text: Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.

“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”

Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines, starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.

blocks.caption: A poster in Siem Reap on Friday shows Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte, flanking Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihamoni, as the capital prepares for the Francophone summit. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.

Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea, where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.

The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.

blocks.caption: Passengers arrive at Shenzhen airport ahead of the Apec summit.   Photograph: Ng Han Guan/AP

blocks.text: Global pivots towards Asia

For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.

Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.

Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.

“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.

blocks.caption: Protesters in Manila make their feelings known before the arrival of Donald Trump for the Asean meeting.  Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPA

blocks.text: Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.

Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas. Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.

A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore.

Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration. Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.
Additional research by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: LIST: Personal information possibly exposed in gov’t data leaks
articles.summary: Despite the Data Privacy Act requiring prompt data breach disclosures, most affected state agencies have yet to inform the public

blocks.text: Despite the Data Privacy Act requiring prompt data breach disclosures, most affected state agencies have yet to inform the public

items: Recent data breaches have exposed sensitive personal information from approximately 20 government agencies in the Philippines.
The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reported potential compromises of taxpayer and individual profile information, respectively.
The Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (Pagcor) is investigating a breach of its database containing personal information of individuals banned from gaming premises.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines — Sensitive personal information may have been exposed in recent data breaches affecting multiple government agencies.

Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) Executive Director Alexander “Aboy” Paraiso confirmed in a radio interview on Friday, November 13, that personal data from around 20 state agencies were exposed.
As of Tuesday, November 10, only 10 of these agencies had submitted personal data breach notifications to the National Privacy Commission (NPC).

blocks.caption: NPC sounds alarm as 10 gov’t agencies report leaks

blocks.text: Rappler reached out to the 10 agencies identified by the NPC to determine the extent of each data breach.
Based on public advisories, disclosures, and statements, here is what is known so far about the information potentially exposed:
In an advisory released on November 10, the BIR said its initial findings showed that only “certain taxpayer profile information” may have been exposed.
The tax bureau also stated that taxpayer information was not “modified or lost,” and that filing and payment records were unaffected.
But CICC Executive Director Paraiso shared that names, business addresses, and Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN) of around 20,000 to 50,000 taxpayers may have been compromised.
The SEC said it discovered on November 6 that individual profile information from its online platforms and databases may have been compromised.

The commission informed users of its online platforms via email on Monday, November 9, that their full names, usernames, email addresses, mobile numbers, birth dates, genders, addresses, and TINs were possibly leaked.
According to a statement published the same day, SEC explained that company records and passwords were not exposed in the breach.
In an advisory released on Wednesday, November 11, Pagcor said it was investigating a potential breach of its National Database of Restricted Persons (NDRP).
The NDRP contains the personal information of individuals banned from entering and playing in Pagcor-authorized gaming premises in the country.
Presidential Decree No. 1869, or the Pagcor Charter, states that the following persons are included in the NDRP:

items: Government officials and employees
Members of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and Philippine National Police
Persons under 21 years old or a student of any school in the Philippines
Employees of gaming licensees or Gaming Employment License holders

blocks.text: It also includes the names of individuals under voluntary or family-applied exclusion programs.
The same database was hacked last year, with Pagcor sharing that the database contains around 560,000 names and clarifying that these are not “addicted gamblers.”

The remaining seven agencies on the NPC’s list had yet to respond to Rappler’s request for comment as of Sunday, November 15. The NPC and CICC had also not responded to Rappler’s requests for additional information.

Republic Act No. 10173, or the Data Privacy Act of 2012, requires personal information controllers such as government offices to notify the NPC and affected individuals if any of their data may have been compromised.
This story will be updated as more government agencies release information about the data breaches. – Rappler.com
