articles.title: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
articles.summary:
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question

  • Get our

blocks.text: When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down.
Except, this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores.
This is its longtime rival, Myer, where entire floors are seemingly permanently on sale.
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question: is Myer next?
‘Sustained erosion of relevance’
At first glance, Myer’s headline numbers seem to defy the retail gloom, with double-digit sales growth to $4.1bn last financial year.

That lift, however, was not driven by surging demand, but by adding sales from the newly acquired apparel chains, Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E, bought from billionaire businessman Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments.
Meanwhile, to keep registers ringing, Myer employed “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”, according to its annual report, which reduced its profitability.
The department store has also slashed the value of its brands, down more than $200m in one year alone, in an admission that its labels are worth far less than they once were.

Department stores have faced a “sustained erosion of relevance over the past five years”, according to IBISWorld market researchers, as online platforms win over bargain-hunters and specialists like beauty retailer Mecca prove more nimble in capturing shifting tastes.
DJs and Myer, on the other hand, have been weighed down by long-running physical property leases tied to underperforming stores in their sprawling networks.
The era of Australian families being fiercely loyal to either David Jones or Myer is long gone, replaced by a grim battle for both chains to stay relevant.

The stress on big department store profitability has been exacerbated by a period of cost of living pressures that have “entrenched deal-hunting behaviour, reshaping how and when consumers engage with department stores”, according to IBISWorld.
Myer was contacted for comment.
Survival tactic or slow-motion bankruptcy
Myer, however, has a critical advantage over David Jones: time.
While DJs fell into administration under mounting debts, Myer finished last financial year with a $100m net cash buffer, buying management breathing space to fix the business.

It has been reducing store numbers and with it lease liabilities – down to 56 stores from 60 before the pandemic – which is something David Jones is only doing now that it has collapsed into administration.
For the moment, Myer is leaning into the discounts demanded by shoppers, in the hope that more profitable trading conditions will emerge.
Richard Hemming, the editor at Under The Radar Report, says in retail “volume is everything”.
after newsletter promotion
“If you get the volumes through, that customer base will eventually be in a position to pay more, and when volumes and margins both improve, you get that double effect,” Hemming says.

While analysts have mixed views on whether permanent discounting is a smart survival tactic or a slow-motion way to go bankrupt, department stores do need to move huge volumes of stock to keep cash flowing and clear seasonal goods.
They can use those discounts to get more people signed up to their loyalty programs – such as the successful Myer One program – in the hope they will become long term customers.
Hemming sees the upside in Myer’s current pain, noting the retailer is “cleaning house earlier than rivals” precisely because investors have long priced it “like it’s going to go broke”.
Myer is revamping the business to aggressively pursue online sales.
Advantage over old rival
Myer shares have been heavily sold down over the years, and now hover around the 24c mark, representing a fraction of its $4.10 float price from 2009.
It did, however, receive a price bump on the day DJs fell into administration.

With roughly two in five Myer stores sharing a shopping centre with a David Jones outlet, investors are betting the coming closure of 19 DJs sites will hand Myer an easy market-share boost, even as its own long-term turnaround demands further store cuts.
In the short term, the pain is likely to intensify for Myer as the David Jones stores marked for closure are under orders to clear stock with widespread promotions, luring customers.
Broader retail sentiment is also souring, as a string of interest rate rises and escalating cost-of-living pressures force cash-strapped shoppers to pare their discretionary spend.
The Retail Doctor Group’s chief executive, Brian Walker, says the main long-term advantage Myer has over its old rival is financial flexibility.
“Whereas David Jones was incredibly encumbered, Myer doesn’t have that issue right now,” Walker says.
“As we sit here today, Myer is financially stronger, but strategically still pretty vulnerable.”

articles.title: ASEAN’s ‘talk shop’ reputation meets Filipinos’ price worries in Manila
articles.summary: Southeast Asian leaders meet in Manila on Sunday, November 15, to cap the Philippines' ASEAN year that's been knocked off course by the US-Israeli war with Iran, a conflict that drove up fuel prices…

blocks.text: November 15, 2026 | 7:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders meet in Manila on Sunday, November 15, to cap the Philippines' ASEAN year that's been knocked off course by the US-Israeli war with Iran, a conflict that drove up fuel prices globally and made the resulting price squeeze a top issue for the bloc.

Opening the last foreign ministers’ meeting of Manila’s chairship on Saturday, November 14, Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the year had brought “unprecedented headwinds,” led by the crisis in the Middle East, and that the Philippines had kept “pivoting our course” in response.

Philippine households continue to be hit hard by the sprawling conflict in the Middle East, which has driven up fuel prices. Inflation accelerated to 7.8% in October, the highest since February 2023, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.

High prices of goods were also the issue Filipinos most often wanted the country to push as ASEAN host, named by 19% surveyed in a Social Weather Stations poll taken in late March and shared again this week, just above the West Philippine Sea.
ASEAN members imported about half their oil from the Middle East before the war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February and effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz.

An ASEAN pact meant to let members share fuel during supply cuts is still not in force though it remains high on the agenda this week. Only four or five of the bloc's 11 members have ratified it as of late October and any sharing under it would be voluntary and on commercial terms.

Asked how the government would measure the success of the Philippines' year as ASEAN chair, Dominic Xavier Imperial, the government's spokesperson for its ASEAN chairship, acknowledged the region was "still feeling the impacts of the Middle East crisis" and that "additional measures" on energy would be forthcoming.
Tangible benefits

Lazaro told her fellow foreign ministers on Saturday that ASEAN’s work “cannot be measured solely by the meetings we convene or the documents that we adopt,” but by whether it can “deliver tangible benefits to our peoples.”

ASEAN leaders’ main economic deliverable is a region-wide digital economy agreement, due to be signed at the summit, that sets common rules for e-commerce, data and digital payments. Lazaro said it would give small businesses “a smoother path… to sell beyond their home markets.”
The year’s setbacks went beyond the war, the DFA chief added, citing “natural calamities that besieged our nations” and “uncertainties that tested the norms of multilateralism.”
“We must also be clear-eyed about the work ahead,” Lazaro said.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in March said he asked fellow leaders whether they saw the need to postpone the bloc’s scheduled May summit due to the energy crisis brought by the Middle East conflict. Eventually, the government scaled down and shortened the summit into a "bare-bones" program lasting a day and a half.
Manila had made “the difficult decision to recalibrate” its hosting, cutting non-essential activities and moving some meetings online, Marcos told the Cebu summit in May.
ASEAN’s limits

ASEAN, often dismissed as a “talk shop,” holds more than a thousand meetings a year across different levels, but many of the statements and work plans produced are never fully carried out, Anoulak Kittikhoun, a former chief executive of the Mekong River Commission, and Joanne Lin, a former ASEAN Secretariat official, wrote in a column for the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

"Its current system—comprising more than a thousand meetings annually, overlapping working groups and siloed sectoral processes—often generates activity without delivering meaningful outcomes," they wrote.
Additionally, decisions made by the bloc need the consent of all 11 members, and the bloc does not interfere in members’ internal affairs.

As a result, many ASEAN agreements are non-binding and enforcement is weak or absent, researchers Mark Anthony Barral and Francis Mark Quimba wrote for the state think tank Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS).

"The differing threat perceptions and the varying levels of economic developments also lead to divisions among member states, hindering consensus-building and effective policy implementation," the researchers wrote.
On top of this, the "principle of non-interference ... limit ASEAN’s ability to provide a prompt response on emerging issues, such as the tension in Myanmar," they wrote.

articles.title: Mike Morrice — the only candidate on the ballot — wins Green Party leadership with 96.6% of vote
articles.summary: The Green Party of Canada enters a new era with former MP Mike Morrice taking over the political party's top job.

image.caption: Mike Morrice at a news conference in Ottawa in November 2023. Morrice will be the next leader of the Green Party of Canada. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking
The Green Party of Canada enters a new era with former MP Mike Morrice taking over the political party's top job.
Greens enter new chapter with Morrice as leader
Mike Morrice, the only candidate in the running, has secured 96.6 per cent of the vote to become Green Party leader, the federal party has announced.
The Greens released the results of their five-month leadership race on Saturday evening. Party members had the option of voting for Morrice or selecting none of the above.
The total number of votes cast was not immediately available.
The party's search to find a new leader began in June. The second candidate in the race, Nira Dookeran, dropped out in September.

items: Former MP Mike Morrice only Green Party of Canada leadership candidate after Nira Dookeran withdraws

blocks.text: Morrice was elected to Parliament in 2021. The one-term MP for the Ontario riding of Kitchener Centre lost his seat last year to a Conservative by a margin of 358 votes.
Soon after the defeat, Morrice was named deputy leader of the party and declared the next Green candidate for Kitchener Centre.
In a news release, the Green Party of Canada said Morrice's campaign brought "renewed energy" to the party.
"Young Greens membership more than doubled, accounting for over 25 per cent of all new members. Overall party membership grew by nearly 20 per cent," the release said.
His campaign also raised more than $113,302.04, which the party said is seven times the required amount.

items: Green Party of Canada begins search for Elizabeth May's replacement

blocks.text: Elizabeth May announced she would be stepping down as party leader after the 2025 federal election, while staying on as the party's sole member of Parliament.
The 2025 election saw the party's national vote share drop below two per cent for the first time in 25 years. Co-leader Jonathan Pedneault failed to secure a seat and resigned.
May was first elected Green Party leader in 2006 and stepped down in 2019. She returned to lead the party in 2022, following the resignation of Annamie Paul.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
articles.summary: Eleven countries took part in the competition in Bangkok. Teenage winner Carmelle Collado's winning dance song is a tribute to Filipino women.

image.caption: Carmelle Collado is the first Eurovision Asia championImage: Sakchai Lalit/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Phillippines on Saturday became the first winner of the Asian version of the Eurovision Song Contest.
Who took part in the event and which songs were featured?

Eleven countries, including South Korea, Malaysia and Vietnam, took part in the song contest in the Thai capital, Bangkok. However, major nations in the region such as China, Japan and India were absent from the event.
19-year-old Carmelle Collado's dance song "Sobra-Sobra" (Too Much) won the competition. The song, which features lyrics in both English and Tagalog, is an empowering tribute to Filipino women.
The Philippines received 211 points in the competition, with Thailand in second place with 170 points. Vietnam placed third with 164 points, while Malaysia landed in fourth place on 152 points.

blocks.caption: Thai duo Mang X Daou came in second place with their romantic pop tune 'Aroma' Image: Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP

blocks.text: National juries in the participating countries and the viewing audience awarded the points.

blocks.caption: Vietnam's Toc Tien performed the lively song 'Em Tien' on leaves of the lotus, a flower associated with her country Image: Sakchai Lalit/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The competition featured motifs inspired by host city Bangkok, with the participants making their way to the stage on tuk-tuks and waving the flag of the countries they represent in a parade.

blocks.caption: Malaysia's Aina Abdul performed the ballad 'Bluest Sky' with water being used to represent the song's emotional buildup Image: Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP

blocks.text: Will the Eurovision Song Contest Asia become a sensation?
The contest featured some references to the camp European competition. Bulgarian singer Dara performed "Bangaranga," the song which won the Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna in May.

It's unclear whether Eurovision Song Contest Asia will be as popular as the original competition, which received 131 million viewers this year. Tickets for the Bangkok event were still available just hours before it kicked off.
In 2022, a US spinoff, the American Song Contest, featured acts from all 50 US states. The competition, hosted by rapper Snoop Dogg and American Idol star Kelly Clarkson, only lasted for one season.

blocks.text: Montreal

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is in Cambodia to attend a summit of the international body of French-speaking states and governments. Quebec, Canada and New Brunswick all have the right to vote in Monday's election to choose a new secretary-general.
Quebec, Canada and New Brunswick all have right to vote in election for new secretary-general
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 14, 2026 5:35 PM EST | Last Updated: 6 hours ago
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is further distancing himself from the Canadian government in his first international outing since winning last month's provincial election.
He suggested Saturday that he was prepared to vote differently from Canada in the election for secretary-general of the Francophonie.
St-Pierre Plamondon is in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, to attend a summit of the international body of French-speaking states and governments.
Quebec, Canada and New Brunswick all have the right to vote in Monday's election to choose a new secretary-general.

Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda is seeking a third term as head of the organization, and is running against Juliana Amato Lumumba of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Dacian Ciolos of Romania, and Coumba Bâ of Mauritania.
St-Pierre Plamondon hasn't said who he'll support, but said he won't necessarily align with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt.

items: Tensions between PM, Quebec premier continue to flare in new tiff over U.S. relations

blocks.text: “We’re not bound by another candidate’s vote,” he said, adding that discussions are ongoing among member states.
Mushikiwabo has expressed her desire for support from Quebec, saying she maintains “very good relations" with the province.
“I would very much like to have Quebec’s support,” she said alongside her deputy, Quebec native Caroline St-Hilaire, whose position is also at stake.
Carney, Quebec premier to have 1st in-person meeting
The topic may be on the agenda as St-Pierre Plamondon and Carney have their first in-person meeting on Sunday.
St-Pierre Plamondon said Saturday that he's optimistic about the discussions, despite his outspoken criticism of Ottawa.
“We’re preparing an (economic) update, so there will be important discussions on that,” he said.
Speaking in the Philippines, Carney also expressed confidence that he and St-Pierre Plamondon will be able to work together.
“I work with all the other premiers in Canada and leaders from countries around the world, so I’m sure we’ll find common priorities,” he said.
Here’s how Quebec plans to ramp up protection of French language
St-Pierre Plamondon began his day in Cambodia by addressing a roundtable of Quebec entrepreneurs, and encouraging them to use the Francophonie to pursue trade opportunities.
He then gave a speech at another entrepreneurs' gathering, where he reminded the attendees that Quebec has been a full member of the Francophonie for over 50 years.
"The (organization) is an example of how we can exercise our sovereignty at the international level," he said.

While Quebec's international relations minister has said the province wouldn't be raising the issue of independence in Cambodia, the premier said his sovereigntist government is sparking interest from other states.

items: Mark Carney's quiet revolution rests on investment and affordability

blocks.text: “I won’t hide the fact that we’ve had ... several hallway conversations in which people are curious because we are the Parti Québécois,” he said.
“So, we discuss the topic of independence, but informally.”
St-Pierre Plamondon has promised his government will hold a referendum on sovereignty towards the end of his term, once U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House.
On Saturday, however, the Quebec premier's appearance on stage drew laughs as he was mistakenly introduced as the prime minister of Canada.

articles.title: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company
articles.summary:
Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable

SpaceX’s megarocket Starship

blocks.text: SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.
The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.

Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the sea as with some previous test flights.
The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.
Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.
The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.

“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday.
This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX, marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.
The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.

SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, chief executive Elon Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes.
Beyond another Moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.

articles.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
articles.summary: SpaceX has performed the historic catch using mechanical arms nicknamed "chopsticks".

blocks.text: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.
"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.
The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:27 local time (21:27 GMT) on Saturday and was successfuly caught.

articles.title: SpaceX carries out first-ever spaceship capture
articles.summary: The successful recovery of the SpaceX Starship marks the first recovery of a spaceship.

image.caption: The SpaceX Starship was an uncrewed mission that launched on FridayImage: Steve Nesius/REUTERS

blocks.text: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned from its longest-yet flight in orbit on Saturday to the tower it was launched from on Friday.

The spaceship descended and smoothly slipped between the mechanical "chopstick arms" above Launch Pad 2 in the US state of Texas. It was the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decadelong effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.
"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted. "Look at her! Baby, she’s back!"

It was the 15th test flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket system. SpaceX had intended to also capture the Super Heavy booster that launched the Starship, but the lower stage recovery was aborted and it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico shortly after launch on Friday.

The successful return of the craft's upper stage after orbiting Earth 14 times for over 22 hours, during which it deployed 26 Starlink satellites, marked a ​key milestone in the multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees ​as key to SpaceX's satellite business and ambitions to put humans on the moon and eventually Mars.
NASA welcomed the news. The US space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base.
"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote on X.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon. The booster's guidance system sensed it was not in the correct position and initiated the self-destruction protocol. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
More to come on this developing news

articles.title: Stranded B.C. flyers out thousands amid flight cancellations due to FAA-ordered ground stop
articles.summary: Some frustrated Air Canada passengers say spotty communication and a lack of rebooking help has left them paying thousands out of pocket amid widespread flight cancellations due to the FAA-ordered…

image.caption: Lisa Dolinski says she had to pay for accommodations out of pocket until the next available alternate flight. (Submitted by Lisa Dolinski)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Some frustrated Air Canada passengers say spotty communication and a lack of rebooking help has left them paying thousands out of pocket amid widespread flight cancellations due to the FAA-ordered ground stop Friday.
Air Canada says it cancelled about 250 flights Friday, affecting roughly 27,000 passengers
Some frustrated Air Canada passengers say spotty communication and a lack of rebooking help have left them paying out of pocket amid widespread flight cancellations.

British Columbians Patricia Arndt, Corey Shack, Nancy Kristoff and Lisa Dolinski were in Cancun, Mexico, celebrating a 50th birthday but had to spend thousands of dollars to stay in Mexico after their return flight was cancelled.
"You just feel lost," said Arndt. "You’re going to have to figure it out yourself."

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop on Friday afternoon due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centres, stemming from a maintenance issue, according to officials.
Air Canada says it cancelled roughly 250 flights Friday, affecting about 27,000 passengers following the FAA's order.
In an email, a spokesperson for Vancouver International Airport (YVR) said there were 54 flight cancellations Friday and another 23 related cancellations Saturday morning.
Unclear updates
Arndt said Air Canada didn’t communicate updated information in a timely manner. The airline told them they would receive an update about rebooking within 30 minutes, Arndt said, but no update came.

The four travellers said their return flight faced a two-hour delay and gate change before they received a text message saying it had been cancelled. They were forced to split up to find accommodations.
Rental cars, trains or Ubers? Airline passengers search for alternatives during U.S. ground stop
Between booking resorts and paying for trips to and from the airport, they estimated each of them spent roughly $2,000 to $3,000, with some families paying even more.
"That was the most frustrating part, because other airlines were communicating with their customers and we were getting zero communication," said Kristoff.
Dolinski woke up first thing Saturday to seek help at the Cancun International Airport, since she said Air Canada’s online platforms weren’t allowing them to book alternate flights home.
Dolinski said the Air Canada line only had one agent tending to it, and they waited three hours before eventually booking an alternate flight home on Wednesday.
Rerouting issues

She said some of her group members booked through Air Canada without extra charge but had to spend money on accommodations, while others paid out of pocket for their flights home but were able to secure a seat on Sunday flights.
McKenzie McMillan, managing partner at Travel Group in Vancouver, said Friday's mass cancellations were unlike anything seen in decades.

items: Passengers and airlines face domino effect after nationwide ground stop in U.S.

blocks.text: "This was a dramatic situation that unfolded yesterday for tens of thousands of passengers," he said.
McMillan says because these cancellations stem from an issue outside airlines’ control, airlines won’t be on the hook to cover those additional costs.

According to the Canadian Transportation Agency, if an airline delays or cancels a flight for reasons outside its control, it's not obligated to compensate affected passengers and the requirement to provide minimum assistance, like paying for food, drink or accommodation, does not apply.

items: Air Canada accused of using 'loophole' to deny compensation

blocks.text: McMillan said even though the FAA lifted its ground-stop order, it will likely take more than a week for airlines to get back to a normal schedule.
Air Canada says it has added flights where possible to help affected passengers, but further disruptions are expected as aircraft and crews remain out of position across its network.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt
articles.summary: The 2027 federal budget proposal has finally been hammered out and is set for a vote in parliament. What are the government's policy priorities in defense, infrastructure, the economy and social…

image.caption: Lawmakers worked through the night to hammer out the details of the federal budgetImage: Carsten Koall/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday morning when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session. Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion). But here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.
Germanys slow road to recovery

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party spoke of a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
Why is debt growing? Crises drive up costs

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities a government and a country set — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.
What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.
Defense spending continues to rise

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June 2026, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary."

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.
How risky is the German government's borrowing spree?
The largest item in the budget: social spending and pensions

Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are plans for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise. People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than one million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.
The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.
Germany is no longer a model of fiscal discipline

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.
German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses
Economic experts warn of rising debt
The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.
German Chancellor Merz vows to push ahead with reforms
The road ahead

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during his visit to Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year."

articles.title: South Sudan pushes back elections amid violent flare-ups
articles.summary: South Sudan has been independent from Sudan since 2011, and has not yet held national elections. Since then, the country faces cycles of violence after a civil war led to a tenuous peace deal.

image.caption: The Republic of South Sudan is Africa's youngest country (FILE: November 15, 2016)Image: Justin Lynch/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Sudan on Saturday pushed back its first national elections from December to February next year, as the country faces flare-ups of violence and political strife.
Why were the elections pushed back?
Presidential and legislative elections are now slated for February 11, 2027.

"We didn't postpone the elections. We have just adjusted the time to allow other processes to be implemented and that is according to the law," National Elections Commission spokeswoman and Commissioner Josephine Achiro said.
"Article 57 of the National Elections Commission gives us authority to adjust the elections timelines," she added.
Achiro said the postponement of the election date is for voter registration and civic education purposes.

According to the World Bank, the vast majority of South Sudanese lack state-recognized ID, creating challenges for voter registration. Thousands of centers have been established across the country to register voters.
What is the political situation in South Sudan?
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in July 2011 following a referendum. The country has some 12 million people and is one of the impoverished nations on the planet.

From 2013 to 2018, forces backed by President Silva Kiir, a member of the Dinka ethnic group, fought against troops supported by Vice President Riek Machar, who hails from the Nuer tribe. More than 400,000 people died in that conflict.
A fragile peace agreement was achieved between the two sides in 2018, with a national unity government established in 2020.

blocks.caption: South Sudanese President Salva Kiir (right in photo) and Vice President Riek Machar are the country's two most prominent political figures and belong to two different ethnic groups (FILE: September 10, 2019)Image: Denis Elamu/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kiir dissolved South Sudan's transitional government in September ahead of elections, and has since ruled by decree in a caretaker administration. He fired Vice President Machar, who had earlier been charged with treason and is under house arrest.
Despite the peace deal, there are also frequent clashes between the Dinka and Nuer groups loyal to Kiir and Machar.
Growing violence

The head of the UN Mission in South Sudan, Anita Kiki Ghebo, said earlier in the week that violence is increasingand added that approximately 10 million people in South Sudan need some form of humanitarian assistance. She also noted that 1.4 million people have entered South Sudan due to an ongoing conflict in Sudan.
"If left unaddressed, political, security, and humanitarian challenges risk reinforcing one another, further exacerbating tensions adn vulnerabilities across the country," she said.

She has urged renewed dialogue "to focus on establishing clear and credible roadmap for completing the outstanding provisions of the Revitalized Peace Agreement," the formal name for the 2018 peace deal.

articles.title: US: Duffy says 'incompetence' or bad tech to blame for flight haltings
articles.summary: Air carriers in the US canceled some 16,000 flights over the past 24 hours in the biggest such grounding since 9/11. Officials hinted that incompetence or faulty equipment, not malfeasance, is the…

image.caption: Transportation Secretary Duffy was asked why updates were carried out on a busy Friday afternoon rather than a time when far fewer flights were scheduledImage: Tom Brenner/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: US Federal Aviation Administration officials and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday said that investigations are ongoing in an attempt to find the cause of the largest mass grounding of flights in the country in over 25 years.

Stranded passengers scrambled to find hotel rooms or buses and trains that could take them to their destinations, others hunkered down in the nation's airports in the first such nationwide grounding since January 2023 and the largest since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks.

International carriers were also forced to cancel flights to the US, and the massive backlog prompted, among other things, the rescheduling of dozens of college and professional sporting events — a staple of many Americans' weekends.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a total of 16,000 flights had been delayed on Friday and Saturday, adding that he hoped flight schedules would be back to normal sometime Sunday, saying the "worst is behind us."
US lifts nationwide air travel ground stop, but disruptions continue
Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks to deflect blame

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said no evidence of malfeasance had been found, before pointing his finger at numerous possible culprits, starting with the previous administration, then Congress and eventually settling on possible "contractor incompetence."

Duffy said the issue may have been a faulty router installed when workers from "legacy contractor" L3Harris replaced aged copper wire with new fiberoptic cable or that they had somehow caused a system overload while updating the wires.

During a press conference that was itself plagued with technical problems, Duffy said, "We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning, was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said, adding that either way, "Our contractor didn't meet the moment."

He was also asked why such complicated updates would be undertaken on a Friday afternoon when air travel is at its busiest rather than on a Saturday night, for instance, when far-fewer planes are in the air. He replied by saying the scheduling of such updates will be reevaluated moving forward.

Since the decision was made to update the very old infrastructure currently in use, Congress has approved $12.5 billion (€11.3 billion) to fund the changeover. The Trump administration had been seeking a further $30 billion to complete the job but Duffy on Friday called $50 billion instead, saying, "This is an emergency."

blocks.caption: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has suggested numerous reasons for the groundings, none having to do with his departmentImage: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who will compensate customers?
Despite the pain and frustration endured by customers, there is also a massive financial component to the groundings.
Since the groundings were ordered by the FAA, airlines are not legally responsible for compensating passengers whose flights were cancelled.

On Saturday, Administrator Bedford said the FAA is "working with aviation stakeholders" to make things right, saying, "everyone will either be reaccommodated (sic) on a flight or they'll get a full refund."

Investors are already beginning to calculate potential losses to airlines — which will compound the sting of sky-high fuel prices brought on by the Trump administration's war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz — with shares of American, Delta and United Airlines falling between 1% and 2% late Friday.
Shares in JetBlue as well as contractor L3Harris were down 3%.

articles.title: Fact check: 'Iranian' content farms reach millions
articles.summary: Several social media accounts claiming to represent the Iranian military show signs of being part of so-called content farms. DW Fact Check looks at how they operate and how users can spot them.

image.caption: The 'Iran Military' accounts share similar names and profile picturesImage: X/TikTok/Instagram

blocks.text: As fears of regional escalation grew after US strikes on Iran, US President Donald Trump claimed the US-Israel war with Iran was "effectively over" on November 9 at a White House briefing. "We're just keeping it the status quo."

Periods of heightened public interest, such as the conflict involving Iran, create fertile ground for so-called content farms. Following Trump's statement, posts on the Iran war surged online again. And a growing network of accounts claiming links to Iran's military has accumulated millions of views.

DW Fact Check examined a number of these accounts and found recurring signs of content farm behavior. Experts who reviewed the accounts DW provided describe them as part of a broader ecosystem of pro-Iran content aggregators that connect across multiple social media platforms.

Content farms are websites or social media accounts, or a network of either, producing large amounts of cheap content in a short time span. They may be driven by economic incentives, but they can also serve as vehicles for political influence campaigns.

blocks.caption: Still under fire: Smoke and fire rise from a commercial cargo vessel following a US military strike on October 10Image: U.S. Central Command/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Content farming and the Iran war
The internet watchdog NewsGuard has found 165 false claims about the Iran warthat collectively have been watched hundreds of millions of times. Only a few of them originated from Iranian state media.
NewsGuard identified the majority as pushing a pro-Iran agenda, shifting toward AI-generated images, and increasingly claiming that accurate stories from authentic media are AI-generated and false.

An analysis by the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) identified pro-Iran networks of X accounts which revealed signs of coordination, cross-promotion and engagement tactics while spreading misleading and AI-generated war content. It found no links to state-affiliated actors.

Several accounts identified by DW Fact Check use the Iranian flag as their profile picture and a variation of "Iran Military" in their username. While ownership cannot always be verified, they share recurring characteristics commonly associated with content farms.
A network reaching millions

Content farms use repetitive and formulaic posting formats, as they are cheaper and easier to produce. Their posts frequently start with the word "BREAKING" and imitate the appearance of news updates on the conflict.

blocks.caption: The account 'Iran Military Media' has over 292,000 followers on X, 597,000 on Facebook and 17,200 followers on InstagramImage: X

blocks.text: One account, called "Iran Military Media," is linked to a Facebook account that Iranian state media have verified as authentic. It has built a substantial audience across multiple social media platforms, with over 290,000 followers on X, 597,000 on Facebook and 17,200 followers on Instagram.

It posts a handful of times a day, often sharing AI-generated or AI-enhanced videos and frequently adopting the "BREAKING" format. Since late 2025, it has published more than 1,600 posts on X, generating over 150 million views and 3.6 million likes.

"The accounts discussed are a central part of this ecosystem as they distribute the pro-Iranian content, state and non-state allied media at relatively low cost and generate millions of views," said Moustafa Ayad, an expert in online influence operations at the ISD.
Iran's 'soft war'

Ayad examined 10 similar "Iran Military"-themed accounts during the same period, and their combined reach is even greater. Together, they accounted for 12,588 posts, 353 million views and 6.6 million likes.
This network is replicated on Facebook in numerous languages. According to Ayad, this strategy is part of what the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei outlined as "soft war."
Ayad said the accounts' reach is amplified when they are paired with other accounts. Only a small share of "Iran Military Media's" 150 million views came from reposted content.
False narratives
A second account, "Iranian Force," has amassed more than 248,000 followers. It typically posts around 10 times a day, though on some days the volume exceeds 30 posts.

blocks.caption: Frequent AI-generated posts are part of the output of the 'Iranian Force' accountImage: X

blocks.text: Like "Iran Military Media," it frequently relies on "BREAKING" alerts and AI-generated content. It also includes genuine footage, often framed through a pro-Iran lens.

X lists the account as being based in Pakistan and its profile history shows six username changes. In a break from the Iran-related content, one post suddenly defends a Pakistani TikToker and includes an appeal in Urdu to the government in Pakistan.

Charlene Lin, an analyst for the internet watchdog NewsGuard, told DW it had flagged this account for multiple false narratives. According to Lin, it is also linked to another account that spreads the same false narratives in coordination.
Unverified claims
A third account, called the "Iran Army," posts a handful of times a day, including AI-generated videos. Its posts regularly reach tens and at times hundreds of thousands of views.

Like "Iranian Force," it distributes videos from official briefings by the Iranian Armed Forces while also using the "BREAKING" format to drive engagement. One post claiming "the war has officially started" received over 41 million views.
Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers

While these accounts differ in reach and post slightly different content, they share many characteristics. The accounts repeatedly share cheaply produced images, at times coordinated between accounts, and make sensational and unverified claims portraying Iran as militarily powerful or politically influential.

Several accounts in this wider ecosystem have faced restrictions. Since March, a number of prominent "Iran Military"-themed accounts have been suspended on X, including "Iran Military Monitor," which had close to 2 million followers before its removal.
A consistent pro-Iran framing
Earlier this year, Iranian state media issued a statement distancing itself from a range of "Iran Military" accounts circulating on social media, stating that only one account was authentic.

Yet for social media users, distinguishing that account from the others may not be straightforward. The verified account uses the same "Iran Military" branding and a similar profile picture, while also sharing AI-generated content and frequent "BREAKING" updates.

blocks.caption: Online and offline, Iran invokes hostility toward the US and Israel. This photo shows a demonstration in Tehran on November 4, featuring an AI-generated imageImage: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: Despite differences in authenticity and affiliation, many of these accounts consistently adopt a pro-Iran framing. They portray Iran as militarily capable, able to retaliate against adversaries and enjoying international support, while rarely highlighting information that contradicts that image.

DW Fact Check found repeated postings of the same content close in time across the accounts and different platforms. The "Iranian Force" and "Iran Military Media" accounts have, for example, posted the same image (here and here), with the same caption on the same day, as have accounts in the wider "Iran Military Media" network.

"The pro-Iranian ecosystem online is large, multi-layered and cuts across almost all of the various popular social media platforms and messaging services," said the ISD's Ayad. "[It's] a key component to the Iranian government's ability to withstand challenges to its rule both from within and outside, while generating sympathy and connections with other online communities."

articles.title: New Orleans port sues for control of China-linked tanker that crashed into cruise ship
articles.summary: Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city's port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a…

image.caption: The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker ship in the New Orleans, La., on Friday. (Gerald Herbert/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city's port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.
Move comes hours after tanker lost its steering, slammed into docked river cruise boat
All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker.

Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday.

The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million US in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday.
It could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River. (Matthew Hinton/The Associated Press)

The first step is to make sure the 60,500 litres of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said. Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.
The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans.
'I thought I was drowning'
The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told local news outlet WDSU-TV.

The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 19 C.
Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.
People are helped out of the water by responders on Friday. Dozens were hospitalized but none of the injuries were deemed critical. (Devon Flanagan/The Associated Press)

"It's fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn't taste very good," Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.
Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him.
"They taught us not to drown," Knab said.
Tanker ship collides with riverboat carrying 129 people in New Orleans

Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday's nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him.

Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said.

items: 'Miracle on the Mississippi': All aboard river cruise boat survive crash with tanker in New Orleans

blocks.text: "Whether it's 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success," Montroll said.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations.
Tanker owner a subsidiary of Chinese company
The Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-metre-long vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.

The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday.

items: Investigation finds party boat carrying North Vancouver students ran aground due to tampering

blocks.text: Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn't respond to an emailed request for comment.

The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

articles.title: Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia
articles.summary:
Filipino entry, pop and rap song Sobra-Sobra, takes 19-year-old to victory at grand final in Bangkok

Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’…

blocks.text: Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra, to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.
Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising.

The winner, who performs under the single name Carmelle, finished on 211 points, 41 clear of the hosts Thailand, with Vietnam third. She received the most votes from both the national juries and the public ballot.
Carmelle, 19, grew up beside the railway tracks in the Bicol region of south-eastern Luzon and has been competing in televised talent contests since she was 12.
Sobra-Sobra mixes pop and rap, is supported by traditional Philippine instruments, the kubing and kulintang, and is sung in Tagalog and English.
After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women”.
“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told the Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”
“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are,” she told the Guardian before the final. “It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas.”

The show opened with a routine celebrating the host country, in which Muay Thai fighters shared the stage with drag performers on street food carts. The 11 acts were then driven on in tuk-tuks, each carrying their national flag.

Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, a star at home for more than 20 years, performed first, among dancers costumed as lotus leaves. Mang x Daou represented Thailand, a duo assembled for the contest in the host country who performed a duet staged like a musical number.

Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai gave one of the most conventionally Eurovision performances of the night with Ananta Maya, a rock ballad staged with fire imagery and a large heart-shaped structure behind him.

He ended it by appealing for support for his country, which he said was “going [through a] very hard situation”. More than 1,500 people were killed and more than 5,000 were reported missing after a rock and ice avalanche near the Chinese border triggered catastrophic flash floods in August.

Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, originally a nine-member a cappella and beatbox group, sang without a single instrument. Three of their members were left out of the final due to a rule capping each act at six performers on stage.
Nyendra from Bhutan sang dressed in the gho, his country’s national dress for men, against a backdrop of Himalayan peaks. Mongolia’s Beck performed in a reinterpreted deel, also a national costume.
Half the result was decided before the show began. The 11 national juries voted at a dress rehearsal on Friday night and put the Philippines top with 93 points, ahead of Vietnam and Malaysia.
The other half came from viewers around the world, who could vote online but not for their own country, and who were given eight free votes each and the option to buy 10 more.

Laos’s entrant, Thinla, was unable to hear her own music during her performance, and her dress rehearsal was aired once all live performances were over. She finished fifth, with the night’s third-highest public score.
Carmelle receives no prize money but a trophy presented by Dara, the Bulgarian singer who won this year’s European contest, and will perform at Eurovision 2027 in Burgas.
Organisers have said the right to stage future editions will not automatically go to the winner, on the grounds that smaller countries lack the infrastructure.
Some of the clearest echoes of Eurovision’s camp traditions came through those who announced the votes.

South Korea’s jury points were read by Jo Kwon, a veteran pop star who has played Adam in the Korean production of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and the title role in Everybody’s Talking About Jamie.
The Philippines’ were read by Vice Ganda, a gay comedian who is one of the biggest stars on Philippine television.

Meanwhile, the guest performer was the Thai singer Jeff Satur, who reached a wider Asian audience through KinnPorsche, a 2022 series in the genre of male same-sex romance dramas that has a large following across Asia.

Organisers intend the Bangkok show to be the first of many regional editions, with the executive producer, Assaf Blecher, saying that 16 or 17 territories had expressed interest in competing next year, among them China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

articles.title: Italy slaps Meta with €805mn fine over access to Android photos
articles.summary: Italian regulators say Meta accessed photos and multimedia content from Italian users via the Facebook application for Android devices. Meta has not yet commented on the fine or the allegations.

image.caption: Meta's global headquarters are in Menlo Park, California, with the US generally having looser data protection rules than the EU Image: Andrew Schwartz/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Italy's data protection agency said on Saturday that it was imposing a €805 million (around $887.3 million) fine on Meta for violating the privacy of Italian users.
What do we know so far?

Italian regulators say Meta accessed the photos and videos from Italian Android phone users via the Facebook app. The regulators said the privacy infringement was due to a feature on the Facebook app which suggests photos from users' personal galleries which they can then post on the social media platform.
The data protection agency said Meta did this "without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them."
The fine, which is equal to 0.4% of Meta's annual turnover, is the largest-ever imposed by Italian regulators on a big tech company.
Meta has 60 days to disable the camera roll suggestions feature and to separately ask for permission from Facebook users for just that function.

Italy's data protection agency said there a "high number of people affected" by Meta's data privacy infringement "which is still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system."
How tech billionaires threaten democracy
Regulators first launched the investigation into Meta in July 2025, and say the big tech giant has not cooperated during the probe.
Meta could file legal appeal
Meta has not yet commented on the fine or the allegations made by the Italian authorities, but it could file a legal appeal against the financial penalty.
The company has also previously denied using the camera roll feature to train AI models, although this aspect was not being probed by Italian regulators.
Meta's European headquarters is in Ireland and the company has previously argued that the data privacy case should fall under Irish legal jurisdiction.
Italian regulators have rejected this claim.

articles.title: Gorgeous, heartrending Club Kid is hitting Canadian theatres. Read our TIFF review
articles.summary: Hitting Canadian theatres now, Club Kid is without doubt a major work. It was without doubt one of the best films at this year's Toronto International Film Festival. And while there is some doubt…

image.caption: Jordan Firstman appears as Peter in a still from Club Kid, which he also wrote and directed. The story of a reluctant, and surprised, sudden father is one of the strongest films at this year's Toronto International Film Festival. (A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

Club Kid is without doubt a major work. It is without doubt one of the best films at this year's Toronto International Film Festival. And while there is some doubt here, Club Kid just might make you cry.
Debut feature film by writer/director/star Jordan Firstman is a wonderfully weird retelling of an old story

Club Kid follows Peter, played by writer/director/star Jordan Firstman, as he drifts through the drugged-out "Club Kid" haze of an unactualized life. A young man with all of the fluid freedom of bachelorhood, but none of the grounding, concrete value of bounded responsibility.

A totally untethered, totally unhappy thirty-something living in the impressively sized, rent-controlled New York loft of his dead mother. A shiftless manbaby arriving still high to meetings for his party-promoter business, then looking for a reason to even care he's been fired.

Club Kid also follows Arlo (Reggie Absolom). That little broccoli-haired waif shows up on his doorstep 10 years after Peter (who is gay) had a half-conscious, fully regretful orgy with a British woman at one of his parties. The wide-eyed, infinitely vulnerable preteen is ferried there after his mother's sudden death — dropped off by a friend of Arlo's mom, who claims there are no other relatives who could possibly take him in.
She then promptly disappears — despite Peter's loud, confused protestations.

Protests like: He didn't know he had a kid. He's not ready to take care of a kid. Is the kid even in the country legally? And most importantly: isn't it unfair, and terrifying, to have your future colonized and destroyed by the all-consuming, all-hours dependency of a snot-nosed little infant?

OK, that last one might have been subconscious. But they are obviously coded into the fabric of Firstman's feature debut: a drippingly emotional but gobsmackingly genuine mark of a true talent's arrival. A deeply affecting melodrama that feels endearing and comfortingly predictable until it suddenly isn't, Club Kid is without doubt a major work.
It is without doubt one of the best films at this year's Toronto International Film Festival. And while there is some doubt here, Club Kid just might make you cry.
But it's not like you've never seen this movie before. Build out the setup, and you've got a narrative cycle you're probably so unconsciously familiar with you know all the ingredients already.

For example: you've got the sad, disaffected adult without purpose. You see them suddenly forced, against their will, to take care of a child whose equal or greater sadness that mirrors and challenges their own. And then there's the fertile and inevitable ground to showcase the rituals and burden of caregiving — a comedically chaotic slideshow of mishandled domestic duties; frantic, but juvenile attempts to keep this kid alive.

In Club Kid, it's the sort of visuals you'd expect: pizza for dinner — followed by a quick trip to the toilet. A closet full of explicitly graphic T-shirts the little one is too adorably naive to know he shouldn't be wearing. And a host of other foibles that slowly tip the scale from resentment to a realization that there is no greater calling than slavishly attending to that iPad-obsessed burden drooling on your shoulder.

items: The Plague isn't a new Lord of the Flies. It's more terrifying
The Debut is totally going to win an Oscar

blocks.text: If you've seen a movie, you've probably seen it: the Big Daddys, About a Boys, Ups, Brother Bears, Uptown Girls and even the Fagins and Artful Dodgers of Oliver!, singing about turning new leaves and starting new lives to the tune of Reviewing the Situation.

And if you've seen them, you probably know what they gravitate toward: the metaphorical, or literal, self-sacrifices. The martyrization that comes with that adult giving up their prior independent life — or life in general — to mature, and to protect the wider future this kid has come to represent.

When it comes to Club Kid, don't worry — none of these are spoilers, despite them being part of the genre I've taken to calling "sad men stealing sad kids." That's because, despite the opening setup and a superficial adherence to a form of melodrama at least as old as 1921's The Kid and 1861's Silas Marner, Firstman's biggest strength is in how he understands, and subverts, the genre.

Because just as soon as you succumb to the genuinely well-written and genuinely effective tropes — this movie's main filmic inspiration, Firstman told CBC at a TIFF press conference, was Auntie Mame after all — they're skewered. An initially and suspiciously smooth meeting between the two develops, it seems, almost accidentally into something deeper and stranger.

After barely a few days, new father Peter is already monologuing about how easy it is to care for Arlo; that this parenting thing is pretty easy as long as you get him pasta for dinner and read a couple of stories at night. He even goes so far as to say it directly to innocent young Arlo — and, by extension, us — during one of those bedtime stories, explaining between lines that caring for the boy has spontaneously fixed his lifelong self-hatred and self-esteem issues. In under a week.
Firstman holds British actor Reggie Absolom, who plays Arlo, at the Cannes Film Festival in Cannes, France on May 15, 2026. (Valery Hache/AFP/Getty Images)

Arlo, meanwhile, is depicted as preternaturally mature, with an openness to everyone and fully developed music taste featuring Elliott Smith and the Cocteau Twins. Incredibly, he seemingly harbours no lingering trauma over his mother — who ostensibly died by suicide just weeks earlier, in an environment we soon learn hid even more horrors.

Instead, Arlo calls Peter "dad" easily and unprompted — all this good-nature barreling forward in a way that might suggest Club Kid is merely speed-running the genuinely efficient, if numbingly cliché, blueprint of these melodramas.

Later, a terrifying and inexplicable action in a public park turns all those assumptions on their head. An intentionally cryptic one, followed by a series of subversions that question Peter's actual suitability as a parent, while intentionally keeping Arlo's interiority a mystery. Subversions suggesting the boy is deeply wounded and unsettled by trauma he's gone through — while keeping even us at arm's length.
Trauma that shows Peter has not — and cannot — understand the depth and breadth of a child's mind through simple paternal displays of affection.

items: A Minecraft Movie is good enough — if you think that's all kids deserve

blocks.text: "I think it was intentional for me, for it to seem like it was easy," Firstman said at the press conference of his decision to work with, then flip, the conventions of these movies.
"Peter is still so immature that he thinks love is enough … but that's not how an adult life works. You have to do the annoying paper work, too."

Beyond the riotous comedy, honest performances and uniquely authentic New York party subculture, this is Club Kid's strongest triumph. A story that recognizes the target of its genre: a man finding internal freedom by finally giving up an immature grip on personal freedom. But refusing to do it by turning the engine of that change into a kid-shaped, broccoli-haired prop.
In Club Kid, he is a real kid. He's named Arlo, and he just might make you cry.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.
