articles.title: SpaceX Starship prepares attempt at pinpoint return landing on Earth
articles.summary: SpaceX's next-generation Starship spacecraft cruised around the globe on Saturday nearing the end of its 15th test flight and what the company hoped would be an unprecedented pinpoint return landing…

image.caption: SpaceX's mega rocket Starship lifts off for a test flight from Starbase, Texas, on Friday. The company is hoping for an unprecedented pinpoint return landing at the exact spot in Texas from ‌which it launched. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

SpaceX's next-generation Starship spacecraft cruised around the globe on Saturday nearing the end of its 15th test flight and what the company hoped would be an unprecedented pinpoint return landing at the exact spot in Texas from ‌which it launched.
Company hopes spacecraft will land at exact same Texas spot from which it launched

Starship's uncrewed upper stage is poised to re-enter Earth's atmosphere after nearly a day in orbit and steer back toward its launch tower, then make an engine-controlled final descent into the embrace of giant mechanical arms ​designed to catch the vehicle as it hovers over ​the launchpad.

If successful, it will mark the first round-trip voyage of a vertically launched spacecraft to orbit and back to the very spot where it ​left Earth, achieving a key test of Elon Musk's long-pursued goal of ⁠producing a fully ⁠reusable rocket system.

The towering two-stage rocket's Super ‌Heavy booster — the rocket's bottom half — carried Starship to space on Friday, lifting off from SpaceX's Starbase, Texas, facilities. That booster had failed to return to the launch pad some 10 minutes after liftoff because of an onboard navigation issue, ⁠nixing SpaceX's plan to recover both parts of the rocket for the first time.
Starship, cruising at an altitude of roughly 260 kilometres, is expected to complete 14 orbits around Earth for ‌a total flight time of 22 hours, 32 minutes.

The 15th Starship flight since 2023 became the longest-lasting mission last night, lasting longer than the roughly three-hour trek in its 14th flight in September, when it reached orbit for the first time.

SpaceX has ​spent roughly a decade developing Starship, which billionaire CEO Elon Musk sees as the future workhorse for the company's satellite ⁠business and ambitions to put humans on the moon and eventually Mars.

SpaceX's dominance in the ⁠global launch industry has been centred on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, which has ⁠launched more than ⁠700 times since 2010. That ​rocket's first stage is reusable, but its second stage — the part that delivers payloads into orbit — is ​discarded into the ocean ⁠after each flight.

Starship's Super Heavy booster has been recovered on three previous test flights using the launch-tower catching system, the last such catch occurring in March 2025. The company has not made such a landing since, either because it planned to dunk it in the Gulf waters or because ⁠of an onboard glitch.

articles.title: Carney says he will not boycott APEC 'family photo' with Putin
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will participate in an upcoming group photo with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit out of respect for the host, Chinese President Xi Jinping.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks with the media during a news conference in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, on Saturday. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will participate in an upcoming group photo with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit out of respect for the host, Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Prime minister says he'll appear in summit's group photo 'out of respect' for host China
"Yes, I will participate in the photo out of respect for the host. We’re in Asia," Carney said, speaking in Manila, the Philippine capital, which is one stop on his overseas multi-country tour.
The photo will be taken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen next week. U.S. President Donald Trump is also expected to attend.

With war in Ukraine continuing and the casualties mounting following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Carney was asked why appearing in the photo is the right move. He said Canada's repudiation of Russia is demonstrated through its broader sanctions policy, not from boycotting the photo.

He pointed to the federal government's recent announcement that it will take steps to prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada for next month's world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

items: Carney wraps meetings on security, trade with European leaders in Ireland
Canadian government says Russian players with visas will still be barred from WJC

blocks.text: "Canada stands firmly with Ukraine, firmly with democracy, territorial integrity, rule of law — and all of those put us on the other side of Vladimir Putin's Russia," Carney said.

Faced with a similar decision at last month's G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said she would opt out of taking part in a group photo with her Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
Then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, centre, and other world leaders wave during the family photo at the G20 summit in Osaka, Japan, in June 2019. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
The "family photos" are traditional diplomatic protocol at world summits.

Putin will attend this year's APEC summit hosted by China because unlike last year's host, South Korea, China is not a member of the International Criminal Court, which has issued an arrest warrant for Putin.

Former prime ministers Justin Trudeau and Stephen Harper both took part in family photos with the Russian leader. This will be Carney's first face-to-face encounter with Putin since becoming prime minister.

items: Carney embarks on a worldwide summit tour to build bridges with Europe and Asia

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the White House has confirmed plans for a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin, coming amid recent U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia.
Asked for his thoughts on the trilateral meeting, Carney reiterated support for NATO allies.
"The security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe, for Europe and NATO, not by Russia," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Mayson Maharaj is a producer for CBC's national television program Power & Politics and a writer for CBC's Parliament Hill bureau.

articles.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
articles.summary: Front-runner Carmelle emerges victorious with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra.

blocks.text: Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra
ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondent, in Bangkok and Jack GreyBBC News
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.
Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.
She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.
There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.
Image source, Getty Images
Carmelle was the youngest contestant in the comeptions at 19 years old
Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.
Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.
Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.
And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.

However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performance

blocks.text: Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performance

The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.
Here's how the final scoreboard ended:
1. The Philippines - 211 points
2. Thailand - 170 points
3. Vietnam - 164 points
4. Malaysia - 152 points
5. Laos - 139 points
6. Bhutan - 126 points
7. Republic of Korea - 113 points
8. Mongolia - 94 points
9. Nepal - 69 points
10. Cambodia - 61 points
11. Bangladesh - 35 points
Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.
Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vietnam's Toc Tien came third with 164 points

blocks.text: Vietnam's Toc Tien came third with 164 points
Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.
There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.
Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outing

blocks.text: Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outing
Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England.
"It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie.
"The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.
They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.
For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.
However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.
The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

articles.title: Margaret Atwood joins other bird lovers to fight against a proposed 600-foot tower on Pelee Island
articles.summary: Atwood called the location, which is one road over from the new Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre, "one of the stupidest places on the planet" to put a tower.

image.caption: Margaret Atwood, shown in this file photo, called the proposed location "one of the stupidest places on the planet" to put a tower. (Liam Sharp)

blocks.text: Windsor·New
Atwood called the location, which is one road over from the new Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre, "one of the stupidest places on the planet" to put a tower.
Company responsible for tower says protecting wildlife has been a priority

Canadian author Margaret Atwood is adding her voice to the growing opposition against a proposed 600-foot communications tower on Pelee Island, amid concerns it could pose a threat to migratory birds.
The Pelee Island Bird Observatory (PIBO) is calling on the federal government do an environmental impact assessment before the tower is allowed to proceed.
The observatory says the tower's height, supporting wires and nighttime lighting could make it particularly dangerous for birds migrating across Lake Erie.
According to PIBO, its monitoring programs counted and banded more than 660,000 birds during 2024 and 2025.
A proposed telecommunications tower on Pelee Island is prompting birders — like Margaret Atwood — to push back
Atwood, a longtime supporter of bird conservation, raised the alarm Friday in a Substack post titled "Bird Scary Tower!"
"Pelee Island is one of the stupidest places on the planet to put such a stock-trading tower," Atwood wrote.
She urged readers to sign a letter calling for a federal assessment, arguing the consequences could extend far beyond the island.
The observatory says the proposed location also overlaps federally mapped critical habitat for several species at risk, including the endangered Blue Racer snake.
It calls the proposed location – which one road over from the newly opened Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre – a place "where birds should land, not die."
Company says protecting birds is a priority
In a statement to CBC News, a spokeswoman for DRW, the company responsible for the tower, said they share the community's commitment to protecting migratory birds and the island's environment.
"Protecting wildlife has been a priority throughout the project's planning," Caroline Vasquez said.
She said DRW commissioned an independent environmental impact study and incorporated recommended mitigation measures into the design.
The company also says it has consulted Birds Canada, PIBO and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Margaret Atwood, left, is a long time supporter of bird conservation on Pelee Island. In this 2024 photo, she and observatory chair Deborah Egan unfurled a banner announcing what would eventually become the Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre. (The Pelee Island Bird Observatory)
"We are committed to voluntarily installing best-in-class bird collision mitigation technologies alongside the lighting requirements for aviation security," Vasquez said.
DRW maintains the project has undergone the public consultation process required by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada.
PIBO, however, argues the company's environmental study did not adequately assess bird collisions during migration.
The observatory submitted a request for a federal impact assessment on Oct. 6.
It says the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada is accepting comments until Monday, with a decision on the assessment request expected by Jan. 19, 2027.
With files from Jacob Barker

articles.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
articles.summary: Sotheby's says it will work with the heirs of a family who had previously owned the artwork to try and reach a solution.

blocks.text: Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.
Châtaigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.
But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.
"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."
The painting - whose name translates as Blossoming Chestnut Trees - is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.
Four other owners have had it since before it was put up for auction this year.
Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times, external, has written to Sotherby's.
He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.
The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

articles.title: Family of Watford woman set alight ‘desperate for answers’ after attack
articles.summary:
Appeal for information comes after Brenda Raymond, 80, was set on fire outside her flat on Monday

The family of an elderly woman who was set on fire outside a block of flats in Watford have…

blocks.text: The family of an elderly woman who was set on fire outside a block of flats in Watford have said that they are “desperate for answers”.
Brenda Raymond, 80, was found set alight outside her flat on Caractacus Cottage View on Monday. She was taken to a nearby hospital, where she is in critical condition.
Hertfordshire constabulary have said that a 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson with intent to endanger life but has been released on bail with strict conditions.
Raymond’s family said the attack had left them in “complete shock” and that they were confused over why she was targeted.
In a statement issued via Hertfordshire constabulary, they said: “Words cannot describe how distressing the past few days have been for us as a family.

“Our beautiful, chatty, fun-loving and much-loved Brenda, who loves to keep fit and dancing, has suffered catastrophic injuries in the most devastating of circumstances; circumstances which have left us all in complete shock.

“We simply cannot understand why anyone would have wanted to hurt her in this way. Someone out there knows something. They know what happened to Brenda. We are desperate for answers and are pleading for anyone with information to please come forward.”
The family also asked for their privacy to be respected during this “unimaginably difficult time”.

Police believe that Raymond was attacked as she returned home at around noon, with her attackers pouring some kind of flammable liquid on her before setting her alight. Detectives said that an accelerant was also poured through the letterbox of a nearby flat, but have not officially linked the two events.
The decision to publicly name Raymond was made by police with the blessing of her family on Wednesday in the hope that it would lead to anyone with knowledge of the attack coming forward.
DI Adam Bridges, from the Major Crime Unit, said: “This was an appalling and deeply distressing attack on an elderly woman who suffered horrific injuries after being set alight outside her own home.
“Our thoughts very much remain with Brenda and her family as we continue to do everything we can to find out what happened and who is responsible.
“Her family are understandably distraught and have taken the step of releasing her name and photograph to help jog people’s memories around this distressing and highly unusual incident.

“Someone out there knows something. You may have witnessed suspicious activity, heard a conversation, noticed unusual behaviour, or captured something on CCTV or dashcam footage without realising its significance.

“Please do not assume that what you know is too small or unimportant to tell us about. It could be a seemingly insignificant piece of information that provides investigators with the breakthrough they need.

“If you know anything about what happened to Brenda or think you may have information that could assist our inquiries, please come forward. Your information could be crucial in helping us find answers and bring those responsible to justice.”

articles.title: COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal
articles.summary: The UN climate chief warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.

image.caption: Protesters outside the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, lament the lack of progress on climate change Image: Umit Bektas/REUTERS

blocks.text: The United Nations' top climate official urged negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to "avoid tactical delays" that would prevent a deal to stop global warming.
Delegates from more than 200 nations are gathered in the Mediterranean city of Antalya with the core goal of preventing the planet from warming by 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit).
Downtown, thousands of civil society and environmental activists from around the world protested against the consequences of climate change.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?
What did the UN climate chief say?
Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), said getting an agreement is "tough but vital work."
"There ​is no collective success without compromise from every party," he added.
"As we head into the second week, ​I urge ‌parties to move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays."

blocks.caption: Unlike previous UN climate summits, expectations for COP31 are mutedImage: Murad Sezer/REUTERS

blocks.text: Climate crisis pushed down agenda

With inflation, wars, deindustrialization and debt being seen as bigger immediate threats, many governments are watering down their commitments to the clean energy transition, along with the billions required to help developing nations to adapt.
The United ⁠States has snubbed the talks ​for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
Delegates also face pressure from large fossil-fuel-producing nations to avoid setting stricter targets for a faster phase-out of oil and gas.
Climate advocates in Antalya are growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of commitment and delaying tactics preventing an ambitious deal.
COP31 is seeking to unlock finance and investment, reduce the use of so-called super-pollutants and methane and ensure food security.

blocks.caption: The COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, runs until November 19Image: Ozan Kose/AFP

blocks.text: Turkey seeks electrification deal
Host Turkey is, meanwhile, pushing a plan to expand global electrification. Yet, some environmental groups are disappointed the proposal doesn't push increased electricity use from renewable sources.
A UN report last month warned that, within a few years, the world is set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming threshold, set in Paris in 2015.
This is the figure most scientists believe should stop the worst effects of climate change.
A first draft of a deal text is expected to emerge next week, according to Australia's ​COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.
Climate protest draws activists from around the world
Meanwhile, tens of thousands of protesters marched through Antalya on Saturday for climate protection and human rights, according to the organizers.
Many were dismayed at the lack of progress and how the climate crisis is taking a back seat.

"The pursuit of profit at all costs continues to set the [global] agenda [and] govern the trajectory of our world, so there is a need to push back," environmental activist Zaki Mamdoo from South Africa told DW.
Luisa Nebauer, the main organizer of Germany's Fridays for Future movement, lamented that Chancellor Friedrich Merz was absent from the conference, along with several other European leaders.
"We won't have a chance to solve any of the crises as long as our planet is destabilizing by the hour," Nebauer told DW. "We must show up!"
Turkish authorities permitted the rally to go ahead, in a country that often bans large public gatherings.
Alongside the march, a parallel "People's Climate Summit" involving hundreds of domestic and international civil society groups takes place in Antalya this weekend.
As Turkey hosts COP31 its beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles

articles.title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
articles.summary: The US government is trying to find out whether the chaos was caused by "incompetence" or faulty equipment.

blocks.text: 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop
ByGeorge Wright and Helen Davidson
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.
Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.
The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.
Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.
Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.
The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added.
"It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.

The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.
Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Duffy told a news conference that the US government did not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Duffy told a news conference that the US government did not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack
No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday.
More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues.

In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.
Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.
Questions remain on why US ground stop happened when it did, former TSA boss says

Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"
A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.

articles.title: Change to Ontario's 'safer-supply' opioid prescriptions abruptly paused due to legal challenge
articles.summary: A controversial change to "safer-supply" opioid prescriptions in Ontario that would force recipients to take them in front of a pharmacist, rather than on their own schedule at home, has been…

image.caption: Hamilton resident Aaron Simkin is relieved a controversial drug prescription policy change has been paused, as he credits take-home prescription opioids with stabilizing his life. (Saira Peesker/CBC)

blocks.text: Hamilton·Breaking

A controversial change to "safer-supply" opioid prescriptions in Ontario that would force recipients to take them in front of a pharmacist, rather than on their own schedule at home, has been abruptly paused due to a legal challenge. Critics said the proposal would drastically affect the lives of drug users while causing potential chaos at pharmacies.
Change was set to start Monday; prescription recipient Aaron Simkin calls pause 'good news'

A controversial change to "safer-supply" opioid prescriptions that would force recipients to take them in front of a pharmacist, rather than on their own schedule at home, has been abruptly paused due to a legal challenge.
The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO) announced the pause Friday, days before the changes were to come into effect on Monday.

The medical regulator, which governs prescription policy for doctors, said it was served with a legal challenge Friday that included a motion for an injunction to halt the changes. An injunction is a court order that forces an entity to do something specific ordered by the court. CPSO says it agreed to pause the changes to allow time to respond to the injunction.

"We recognize that physicians may already have been working with patients and other members of their care teams in preparation for November 16," the release said. "During the pause, physicians should continue to practise in accordance with their professional obligations and exercise clinical judgment based on the individual circumstances and needs of their patients."
CPSO did not respond to a request for more information ahead of publication.

The CPSO announced Oct. 13 that its board had voted for the proposed changes. In addition to eliminating take-home doses of opioids, the changes would require physicians to assess patients receiving the drugs at least once a month in person, and that people on the drugs should also be prescribed a long-acting opioid, such as methadone or suboxone, widely used therapies for opioid addiction.

The college said the proposed changes would "strengthen expectations for physicians who prescribe safer supply medications" and help prevent the drugs from being used by people for whom they aren't prescribed.

"The diversion of safer supply medication raises serious concerns for patient and public safety," said Dr. Nancy Whitmore, registrar and CEO, in a release. "These amendments… represent meaningful regulatory action within CPSO's mandate to serve in the public interest."
Hamilton prescription opioid recipient says pause brings relief
Hamilton resident Aaron Simkin, who says prescription opioids helped stabilize his life after many years of homelessness and drug use, called the pause "good news."

Simkin lived at the Hamilton YWCA for four years, and spent most of his time looking for drugs to fuel his addictions. Now, he has an apartment, five cats and four part-time jobs, and credits prescription opioids for helping turn his life around.

"It just stabilized my life because I didn't need to score any drugs," said Simkin, 47. "You don't have to run around looking for people to buy from and… worrying [about getting] fake drugs or fentanyl.
"There's no chaos."

Simkin picks up his prescription, which includes Dilaudid to treat opioid dependence, once a day. He takes the medication every four to five hours, a routine that staves off the physical symptoms of withdrawal. "I'm not getting high. It's just maintaining," he said.

Simkin said the proposed changes would drastically affect his daily routine and lead to long stints where he can't access the drugs, during the hours the pharmacy is closed. He's scared he won't be able to continue to hold down work while in withdrawal, and worries he could return to the black market to make it through.

"It's so hypocritical," he told CBC Hamilton in a Friday interview in a coffee shop near his apartment. "They talk like taking drugs off the street is 'community safety,' but they create a vacuum. They create a black market. It's not safe. The drugs aren't safe."
CPSO says changes will prevent diversion of drugs

In devising the proposed new regime, CPSO says it consulted with "physicians with expertise in addiction medicine and health system partners, including the Office of the Chief Medical Officer of Health."
Rami Safi, a Hamilton pharmacist with several clients who receive these medications, does not believe adequate consultation occurred.

Safi, manager of Wellness Wave pharmacy near Ottawa and Barton streets, said that in addition to impacting patients, the changes also affect pharmacies, social workers and others who provide care for drug users, groups that do not appear to have been consulted.
Rami Safi stands in front of his pharmacy, Wellness Wave, on Barton Street East in Hamilton on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Saira Peesker/CBC)

He said he often sees complaints on social media about drug users loitering around pharmacies, and said the proposed change was bound to increase tension between pharmacies, their customers and others in their neighbourhoods.

"It's going to make it worse because people will just hang out around the pharmacy" between their doses, he said. "This has created so [many] problems for me and for my colleagues across the city. It's an extra pressure that we don't need in these situations."
'Do we ditch them and just say, "Let them die"?'

Safi, who is also a psychotherapist, believes stricter rules — such as the proposed change to safe-supply prescriptions — come from a place of moral judgement of people who use drugs, rather than an approach that would best address the crisis.

"We see it as morality because the consequences of using drugs might lead to crime," he said. "When you see it in your own personal life, you know that it's actually way deeper than that. It's biological factors, it's social factors and it's psychological factors."
After safer-supply prescriptions allowed many drug users to function better within mainstream society, Safi worries the new changes will push them back to the margins.

He'd like to see the health care system redirect its efforts toward better treating the mental-health conditions of people who use drugs, and better-integrated health care where a patient's various practitioners — including doctors, social workers, pharmacists and mental health experts — could work as a team with a shared approach.
Safi pointed to the shocking number of people who have died from opioid toxicity in Canada — 57,509 between January 2016 and March 2026, according to Statistics Canada.

"If you have an army fighting somewhere, you will not lose this number," he said. "Do we ditch them and just say, 'Let them die'? That's what we're kind of doing in a way. Or do we have to find real proper solutions and access to care?"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Saira Peesker is a reporter and producer with CBC Hamilton, with particular interests in climate, labour and local politics. She has previously worked with the Hamilton Spectator and CTV News, and is a regular contributor to the Globe and Mail, covering business and personal finance.

articles.title: NHS England on track to miss key cancer treatment target by 10,000 patients
articles.summary:
Exclusive: 2,850 more patients a month would need to be treated within 62 days to meet March 2027 goal, as experts warn of failure of leadership

Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England…

blocks.text: Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not be treated on time because the government will fail to meet its targets, amid a failure of leadership, focus and resource, experts have warned.

The NHS set an interim target to treat 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referral or consultant upgrade by March 2027. But with little more than 100 days to go, the proportion of patients starting treatment on time in September was 70.7%, down from 71.9% in August, NHS figures show.

Exclusive analysis of official figures for the Guardian reveals the NHS would have to treat 2,850 additional patients on time each month to get back on track, assuming patient volumes remain consistent.

According to calculations by Radiotherapy UK, 24,400 cancer patients a month would need to start treatment on time to hit the 80% target in March. But the NHS is only treating about 21,500 cancer patients a month within the 62-day target, leaving a monthly shortfall of 2,850 and a cumulative shortfall of 9,490 patients, the charity found.

Prof Pat Price, the chair of Radiotherapy UK and a leading oncologist, said: “The government is going to miss its cancer treatment target because the NHS does not have enough staff or equipment to treat the number of patients coming through its doors. This lack of leadership means thousands more people could die because they don’t get their treatment on time.”

The analysis also found significant disparities between treatment of common cancer types. While more than two-thirds of patients with prostate and breast cancers were treated within two months ((70.1% and 68.8% respectively), only 60.9% of those with lung cancer and 60% of those with gynaecological cancers were treated on time. For head and neck cancers, barely half (56.5%) were. Regional inequalities were also stark, the research found. The Midlands had the lowest proportion treated on time, at 66.6%, compared with 77.3% in London.

Mark Lawler, a professor of digital health and chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, believes failures of accountability and focus are to blame. He said: “The whole system is being held together by goodwill glue alone. Lack of leadership is derailing efforts to improve cancer survival. Unless there is accountability for these failures by the NHS, a radical change in mindset and a focus on the basics, we will miss hitting treatment targets for another decade.”

The figures come as analysis of latest cancer diagnosis targets by Cancer Research UK shows that, over the last year, barely half (55.4%) of patients with cancer were diagnosed within 28 days of an urgent referral, against the faster diagnostic standard target of 80%, compared with 79.1% of patients who received the all-clear on time.
after newsletter promotion

Naser Turabi, Cancer Research UK’s director of health policy and evidence, said hospital capacity was not able to keep pace with surging demand for cancer diagnosis – with urgent referrals in England up about 20% over the past four years alone. “While recent investment in diagnostic equipment is welcome, we’re not seeing enough progress to cut waiting times for the 6% of people who go on to receive a cancer diagnosis,” he said.

Dr Hilary Williams, the Royal College of Physicians clinical vice-president and a consultant in medical oncology, said crucial earlier diagnosis was only beneficial if patients could then be treated quickly.

“To close the gap, the NHS needs sufficient capacity across the whole cancer pathway,” Williams said. “That means more diagnostic capacity, including imaging, endoscopy and pathology, alongside the specialist workforce needed to deliver and interpret those tests. It also means enough treatment capacity in surgery, radiotherapy and systemic treatments so that diagnosing people more quickly doesn’t simply move the bottleneck further down the pathway.”

Dr Stephen Harden, the president of the Royal College of Radiologists, said “chronic shortages” of clinical radiologists and clinical oncologists, who diagnose, monitor and treat cancer, were “driving dangerous delays” in diagnosing and treating the disease.

“Perversely, NHS hiring freezes for these doctors have doubled in the last year, making it even harder to keep patients safe,” Harden said. “Technology and new ways of working can relieve pressure to an extent, but fundamentally, rising demand for cancer care has outpaced workforce capacity. The government must now step in to end recruitment freezes and ensure services have the doctors they need to diagnose and treat patients on time.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction, with all three cancer standards better than a year ago, and around 290,000 more people over the last year getting diagnosed on time or having cancer ruled out, compared to the year before the election.

“But we know there is much more to do. Our national cancer plan will help more people to get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner, giving them the best possible chances of recovery and survival.”

articles.title: Democrat wins Alaska governor’s seat for first time in nearly 30 years
articles.summary:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’ victory means Democrats will now hold 30 US governorships after midterm blowout

Democrats have captured…

blocks.text: Democrats have captured Alaska’s governor’s seat for the first time in nearly three decades, marking another major victory for their party in a midterm election period that has dramatically shifted political power across the US.

Former Alaska state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republican opponents, including a candidate backed by Donald Trump, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998.

His victory – called by the Associated Press on Friday, 10 days after the polls closed – adds to a growing list of Democratic gains nationwide, bringing the party’s total to 30 US governorships. Democrats have also taken control of governor’s offices in several other longtime Republican strongholds, including Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
Kreiss-Tomkins, widely known as JKT, secured the win having mounted a political comeback three years after departing the Alaska house of representatives.
The 37-year-old traveled extensively throughout the state during his campaign, building support around economic concerns and a promise to change the direction of Alaska’s government.

His platform centered on tackling affordability, ensuring full funding for public education, and requiring all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income taxes. He also pushed for a temporary halt to new datacenter developments until state lawmakers establish regulations governing their construction.
Throughout the campaign, Kreiss-Tomkins sharply criticized the leadership of outgoing the Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, arguing that Alaska had become “broken” during his eight years in office.
“Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “We’ve been running the same campaign since we launched in February, and I don’t take anyone’s vote for granted.”

Among his criticisms was the deterioration of the state’s ferry system, which Kreiss-Tomkins said had been left in disarray as service to numerous communities was drastically reduced. The ferry network serves as a critical transportation link for communities in south-east Alaska that lack road connections, including some with limited access to air travel.

Despite his criticism of the outgoing administration, Kreiss-Tomkins presented himself as a leader willing to work across political divisions. He pledged to assemble a cabinet that includes Democrats, Republicans and independents.

Unlike most states, Alaska allows voters to rank candidates by preference through ranked-choice voting – a system that also permits multiple candidates from the same political party to run against one another.
But Kreiss-Tomkins avoided the need for additional rounds of vote counting after winning more than 50% of first-choice votes, securing an outright victory.

The Alaska result comes just days after Democrats scored another major gubernatorial win in staunchly conservative Kansas, where the Democratic state senator Cindy Holscher narrowly defeated the Republican state senate president, Ty Masterson.
after newsletter promotion

Masterson, who received Trump’s endorsement, faced a campaign in which Holscher repeatedly highlighted his ties to the Republican president. At the same time, Holscher maintained that she would remain willing to cooperate with the Trump administration on issues where common ground could be found.
The back-to-back victories in Alaska and Kansas underscore the scale of Democratic gains in what has become a nationwide electoral shift.

The party’s long-anticipated “blue wave” has now materialized, with Democrats flipping eight seats in the US Senate, gaining more than two dozen seats in the House and significantly expanding their control of governors’ offices after the 3 November midterms.

Such gains have handed Democrats a strong majority in Congress for the latter half of Trump’s second presidency, delivering a major shift in the balance of power in Washington and state governments across the US.

Meanwhile, with few ballots left to count for Alaska’s midterm US Senate election, Democrat Mary Peltola on Saturday was leading Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan, Alaska Public Media reported. That had prompted MS Now to characterize that Senate race as “leans Democratic”.

Beside Alaska and Kansas, the Democratic party won gubernatorial elections over Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, putting them in control of a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Gina Hinojosa is the first Democrat to be elected governor of Texas in 35 years – and also the state’s first Hispanic governor.

A major factor in the GOP’s midterm defeat is the unpopularity of Trump, whom most Republican lawmakers clung to even as polls indicated voters did not support his immigration crackdown, tariffs, the war with Iran or his signature domestic policy bill.

articles.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.summary: The social media giant is accused of not informing about 20 million users it had access to their photos.

blocks.text: Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment.
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.title: Satisfaction with Marcos government drops anew – SWS
articles.summary: Public satisfaction with the Marcos administration dropped anew in the third quarter survey conducted by Social Weather Stations.

blocks.text: November 15, 2026 | 12:00am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on May 25, 2026.
PCO
MANILA, Philippines — Public satisfaction with the Marcos administration dropped anew in the third quarter survey conducted by Social Weather Stations (SWS).

After recovering to 42 percent in June, the proportion of respondents satisfied with the general performance of the national government again dropped to 38 percent in the poll conducted from Sept. 21 to 27.
Those who were dissatisfied increased from 40 percent to 42 percent, while undecided respondents hardly moved from 17 percent to 18 percent.
This resulted in a net satisfaction rating of “neutral” -4, down from +1 in the June poll.
It was the second lowest for the Marcos administration, after the “poor” -13 it obtained in March 2026.
At the time, 32 percent said they were satisfied and 46 percent said they were dissatisfied with the national government.
The net satisfaction rating is the rounded-off difference between those who said they were satisfied and dissatisfied with the performance of the administration.

SWS classifies net ratings of at least +70 as “excellent”; +50 to +69 as “very good”; +30 to +49 as “good”; +10 to +29 as “moderate”; +9 to -9 as “neutral”; -10 to -29 as “poor”; -30 to -49 as “bad”; -50 to -69 as “very bad”; and -70 and below as “execrable.”
Based on the latest poll, net satisfaction with the government was lowest among those in Metro Manila (-21), followed by those in Mindanao (-17), the Visayas (-2) and the rest of Luzon (+7).
It was also lower among younger demographics and those with college education.
The survey found that the Marcos administration obtained negative net satisfaction ratings in five issues.

It was lowest in terms of fighting inflation (-34), followed by eradicating graft and corruption (-3), fighting crimes (-25), ensuring that oil companies do not take advantage of oil prices (-25) and generating solutions for rising oil prices (-21).

Four issues had “neutral” net satisfaction ratings: preparing for climate change (+2), taking care of Filipinos in war-affected countries (+3), being prepared for strong typhoons (+5) and ensuring that no family will ever go hungry (+6).
Those with “moderate” net ratings include defending Philippine territory in the West Philippine Sea (+18), ensuring efficient public transportation (+23) and ensuring food security (+27).

The Marcos administration had “good” and “very good” ratings in terms of developing science and technology (+30), helping disaster victims (+36), creating policies that generate job opportunities (+40), implementing housing programs (+40), helping the poor (+42), improving the quality of education (+5) and providing basic education in public elementary and high schools (+61).
The survey had 1,500 respondents and a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points for national estimates.

articles.title: Rubio to accompany Trump in Manila
articles.summary: United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio will accompany US President Donald Trump when the latter attends the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in Manila on Nov. 17.

blocks.text: November 15, 2026 | 12:00am
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (Anadolu)

MANILA, Philippines — United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio will accompany US President Donald Trump when the latter attends the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17.
“Secretary Rubio will be joining President Trump,” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez confirmed in a text message to The STAR yesterday.
Romualdez added that Rubio will also join Trump for the Quad leaders’ summit on the sidelines of the key Asian meeting in the country.
This is Rubio’s second visit to Manila this year. He attended the 59th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and related high-level regional summits in July.

During his earlier visit, Rubio disclosed that a US Guard vessel was in the region during the July 20 China Coast Guard baton attack at Ayungin Shoal and helped in the rescue of the injured Philippine Navy personnel for medical treatment.
Rubio also indicated last month that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue leaders will meet on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, which begins today.
It will be the Quad leaders’ first summit since 2024 and the first for Trump in his current term.

The Quad group is a key strategic partnership for cooperation on maritime security. It aims to promote a “free and open” Indo-Pacific and balance China’s expanding military and economic influence in the Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: Diplomats convene ahead of ASEAN meet
articles.summary: Top diplomats of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations convened yesterday to prepare for the opening of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits today.

blocks.text: November 15, 2026 | 12:00am

ASEAN leaders arrive in the country yesterday for the three-day regional summit that kicks off today. Dignitaries include Sultan of Brunei Hassanal Bolkiah (left), Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung (middle) and Lao People’s Democratic Republic Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith (right).
Ryan Baldemor, Noel Pabalate
MANILA, Philippines — Top diplomats of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations convened yesterday to prepare for the opening of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits today.

Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Teresa Lazaro led the last ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting (AMM) yesterday, where the diplomats exchanged views on key regional and international issues, including the region’s external relations and efforts to advance ASEAN Community-building.
In her opening remarks, Lazaro said the Philippines assumed the ASEAN chairship and set sail with a clear course anchored on priorities, but the chairship was not without its challenges.

“Yet, as with any ship sailing through unpredictable waters, the year brought unprecedented head winds, particularly the unfolding crisis in the Middle East, the natural calamities that besiege our nations and uncertainties that test the norms of multilateralism,” Lazaro said.
The secretary said the Philippines is grateful for the trust and cooperation and partnership of all ASEAN member-states.

During the AMM, Lazaro also announced the establishment of the ASEAN Maritime Center in the Philippines which will serve as a knowledge hub and support platform on maritime-related initiatives and issues in accordance with the priorities identified by the ASEAN member-states.
ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn also participated in the AMM.
The ASEAN Senior Officials’ Meeting also convened yesterday to advance preparations for the Summit.
Meanwhile, Lazaro said that 80 percent of the discussions on the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea have been finished.

articles.title: ASEAN ministers sign digital economy pact
articles.summary: Ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) yesterday signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, a priority deliverable under the Philippines’ ASEAN chairship.

blocks.text: November 15, 2026 | 12:00am

Trade and Industry Cristina Aldeguer-Roque joined fellow ASEAN economic and trade ministers for a group photo during the signing ceremony of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) in Manila on November 14.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) yesterday signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), a priority deliverable under the Philippines’ ASEAN chairship.
Speaking at the DEFA’s signing yesterday, Trade Secretary Cristina Roque said the agreement is a landmark achievement, being the world’s first region-wide digital economy agreement of its kind.
As such, it is expected to enable the ASEAN to shape the future of the digital economy.
Roque said the agreement would support ASEAN’s aim to build a more integrated digital economy for nearly 680 million people and potentially double its value to $2 trillion by 2030.
“But DEFA is not simply about economic growth. It is establishing the rules, systems and cooperation that will allow our people and businesses to participate more fully in that growth,” she said.
The agreement will provide a common framework to promote a more seamless, secure and interconnected ASEAN digital marketplace.
Under the agreement, ASEAN members will work together on key areas such as digital trade and cross-border e-commerce to make it easier for businesses to offer goods and services across the region.
Roque said the agreement can also help open employment opportunities in e-commerce, information technology-business process management, digital services and the creative industries.

Asian Development Bank president Masato Kanda said during the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit yesterday that the multilateral lender is providing up to $5 billion by 2030 to support the implementation of the DEFA.

“ADB is pledging up to $5 billion by 2030 to help ASEAN turn its DEFA into action: digital infrastructure, cross-border data and payments, cybersecurity, AI readiness and digital inclusion,” Kanda said.

At the same event, Kanda announced the ADB will help strengthen the region’s water and food security through the ASEAN Resilient Rivers Initiative, which aims to mobilize up to $8 billion in public and private financing by 2030.
He said these two initiatives complete ADB’s $30-billion pledge by 2030 announced last May to support the ASEAN’s development priorities.

articles.title: Callamard returning to Philippines to meet drug war victims
articles.summary: Former United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial killings Agnès Callamard will return to the Philippines for the first time since 2017 to meet with victims of the Duterte…

blocks.text: November 15, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Former United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial killings Agnès Callamard will return to the Philippines for the first time since 2017 to meet with victims of the Duterte administration’s bloody war on drugs.

Callamard, now secretary-general of human rights organization Amnesty International, will be in the country from Nov. 19 to 22, two months after the Marcos government lifted the Duterte-era immigration ban that prevented her from entering the country.

“I’m delighted to be able to return to the Philippines, a country close to my heart where I have many friends. I am moved to meet once again with victims and survivors of Duterte’s so-called ‘war on drugs’ and pay tribute in person to their incredible courage and resilience,” Callamard said in a statement.

“This long overdue visit comes at a historic time, with Duterte finally set to go on trial in The Hague for the crime against humanity of murder. Without the determined efforts of the Filipino people, lawyers and civil society, this powerful exercise in international justice would not have been possible,” she added.
A fierce critic of the drug war, Callamard repeatedly drew the ire of Duterte for her strong rebuke of the human rights violations during his administration.
She visited the Philippines in 2017 to attend an academic conference, prompting the Duterte government to issue an immigration ban.

articles.title: Experts weigh in on Pax Silica opportunities, costs
articles.summary: Experts from the University of the Philippines shared their perspectives on the proposed Pax Silica initiative, examining its potential implications for the Philippines to better understand what it…

blocks.text: November 15, 2026 | 12:00am

Riders pass by a mural by visual artist Sim Tolentino depicting US President Donald Trump as an artificial intelligence cyborg at the University of the Philippines Diliman freedom wall in Quezon City on November 14, 2026.
Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — Experts from the University of the Philippines shared their perspectives on the proposed Pax Silica initiative, examining its potential implications for the Philippines to better understand what it could mean for the country.
In a forum entitled, “PAX SILICA: Progress for Whom?” UP School of Economics Professor Cielo Magno examined Pax Silica in the context of global competition over critical minerals.
She noted the country’s position in the global nickel industry, noting that the Philippines and Indonesia together account for more than 70 percent of global nickel production.
However, much of the nickel produced in both countries goes to China for processing.

“Of the 20 critical minerals needed for the energy transition, China controls the processing of 19. Against this backdrop, we can better understand the United States’ interest in the Philippines,” Magno said.

She said that although the memorandum has not yet been made public, she said she learned from contacts at the Department of Environment and Natural Resources that the agreement would reportedly give the US first access to mining areas in the Philippines.

“I have been discussing mining for over a decade and the conversation about downstream processing has gained momentum. How do we maximize this opportunity, and how will we, as a country, benefit?” Magno said.

For her part, Jelaine Gan of the UP Diliman Institute of Biology explained that, under the Pax Silica initiative, the Philippines’ strengths lie in its critical minerals, talent and strategic location.

“The proposed site for Pax Silica covers approximately 3.3 times the area of UP Diliman. Allocating land for one purpose means displacing other uses. This land is used for agriculture by Indigenous communities,” Gan said.

She noted that according to the Bases Conversion and Development Authority, the proposed site would require 65 to 90 million liters of water per day, noting that this is equivalent to approximately 26 to 36 Olympic-sized swimming pools daily. — EJ Macababbad, Alexis Romero

articles.title: PH, Brazil seek agricultural cooperation to protect livestock
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva have discussed strengthening agricultural cooperation to protect local farms and support food security, the…

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva have discussed strengthening agricultural cooperation to protect local farms and support food security, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said Saturday.
Lula, who is in the Philippines for the 49th ASEAN Summit, met with Marcos to discuss livestock production, animal health and agribusiness, among other areas of cooperation, according to the Palace.

articles.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
articles.summary: The foreign ministry in Abuja says 6 Nigerians with underlying health problems have died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

blocks.text: Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.
The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.
Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.
The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.
It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.
The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.
Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.

This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association.

The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people - which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

articles.title: 3 kids, 2 adults in life-threatening condition after Burlington, Ont., house fire: police
articles.summary: Five people, including three children, are in life-threatening condition in hospital after a house fire in Burlington on Saturday morning, Halton police say.

image.caption: Two adults and three children were taken to hospital in life-threatening condition Saturday morning after a house fire in Burlington, said Halton police. (Spencer Gallichan-Lowe/CBC)

blocks.text: Hamilton·Updated
Five people, including three children, are in life-threatening condition in hospital after a house fire in Burlington on Saturday morning, Halton police say.
Paramedics say they transported a 6th person to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries
Five people, including three children, are in life-threatening condition in hospital after a house fire in Burlington on Saturday morning, according to Halton police.
Emergency crews responded to a fire at a townhouse complex near Maple Crossing Boulevard and Freeman Street around 6:50 a.m., Halton police Const. Ryan Anderson told CBC News at the scene.

Burlington fire crews quickly extinguished the blaze and rescued two adults, a child aged about 12 and two children under the age of 5, he said. Anderson wasn't able to confirm if the five residents were related.
"It's a really, really tragic scene out here," he said.

Halton paramedics said all of the injuries were related to the fire. They said a sixth person was also taken to hospital in non-life-threatening condition. Police were not able to confirm if that person was a resident in the home.
The fire was contained to one unit of the complex, Anderson said. Other homes did not need to be evacuated, he said.
Burlington Fire Department, the Office of the Fire Marshal (OFM) and Halton police are investigating the fire, he said.

Three patients were initially reported as vital signs absent after a house fire, but are now in critical condition at the hospital, said Burlington Fire Chief Drew Boys on Nov. 14, 2026. (Spencer Gallichan-Lowe/CBC)
In its early stage, the investigation has not ruled out any factors, including whether the fire was suspicious or whether fire alarms were working, he said.

Three patients were initially reported as vital signs absent, but are now in critical condition at the hospital, Burlington Fire Chief Drew Boys said at the scene. Emergency crews conducted CPR at the scene and en route to the hospital, he said.
He urged residents to ensure their homes have a working fire alarm on every level and to practise a fire safety escape plan with their families.
OFM investigators are at the scene to determine the safety of the structure and to determine the origin and cause of the fire, said spokesperson Jim Demetriou at a news conference at the scene.
"Our thoughts are with the families affected by this tragic incident," he said.
OFM spokesperson Jim Demetriou urged people to check if their homes have working fire alarms and to routinely practice safety plans with their families. (Spencer Gallichan-Lowe/CBC)
Neighbours shocked, hope for best for victims

Neighbour Sasha Guerriero said she woke up Saturday morning to the smell of smoke and the sounds of smashing glass and people yelling. She said she evacuated her home with her adult son just as fire crews were pulling the children out of the home.
"It's probably one of the most traumatizing things I've ever seen. It's awful," she said, adding she doesn't know the residents, but has played with the kids when they run around outside.
"The kids are lovely. Really good, nice kids."
The residents of the home had moved to the area about five to six months ago, said neighbour Bonnie Labocha.
"I was shocked," she said, adding her granddaughter sometimes plays with one of the children.
She said she feared the worst when she saw emergency crews conducting CPR outside of the home, but was relieved to see paramedics attach IVs before taking the victims to hospital.

articles.title: Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim
articles.summary: DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

image.caption: Jaafar Abdul Karim (left) and Katja Gloger were the proud winners of the award for outstanding international journalismImage: Sven Moschitz

blocks.text: At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.
Germany's public broadcasters under fire from far-right AfD

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.
Call for more international coverage

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.
Why press freedom matters to everyone, not just journalists

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.
Belief in the power of dialogue

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

blocks.caption: 'When everyone jumps to conclusions, we need journalists who ask questions first,' said DW's Jaafar Abdul KarimImage: Sven Moschitz

blocks.text: Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."
This article was originally written in German.
