articles.title: What's going on with the polar vortex?
articles.summary: Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it…

image.caption: Cold snaps during winter can sometimes be linked to disruptions to the polar vortexImage: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.
If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.
Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.
Earliest vortex disruption on record
It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.
The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

blocks.caption: When the polar vortex is detabilized, it can send a blast of freezing temperatures further southImage: Adam Glanzman/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: What exactly is the polar vortex and how does it work?
The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.
So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.
This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.
It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.
What does this mean for winter weather?

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.
Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.
For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.
What happens when El Nino meets climate change?

articles.title: Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany
articles.summary: Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two…

image.caption: While the Russia-based KHL remains one of the world's top leagues, Russia has been excluded from international play for yearsImage: Peter Kovalev/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

blocks.caption: Vladislav Tretiak, head of the Russian Ice Hockey Federation, was the Soviet Union's top goalie in the 1970s and early 1980sImage: Yuri Kochetkov/SNA/IMAGO

blocks.text: "There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.
"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."
Canada refuses to bend on junior tournament
The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's Secretary of Sport, said in a statement. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.
On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors

and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.
Men's tournament with Russia 'effectively impossible'

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14. With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."
However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport said on Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the (German) ice hockey federation (DEB), nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a World Championship anywhere."
At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport—and ice hockey in particular—find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."
Munich's Olympic bid and the IOC's new stance on Russia

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hardline on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to pointing the way forward for the men's tournament in Germany next May.

articles.title: Watch: Divers explore US ship sunk off Florida coast to create new reef
articles.summary: The ship was intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida in order to create the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

blocks.text: The ship, which was once the fastest in the world and longer than the Titanic, was intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida, in order to create the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sea life and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila
articles.summary: Leaders and representatives of the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and their allies, are gathering in Manila for the bloc's biggest event of the year

blocks.text: The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.
The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.
During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

Check out this page for the latest ASEAN Summit news, photos, videos, and insights. For more updates and to share your own views, you can also join the Security and Global Affairs chat room in Rappler’s Muni app.

articles.title: Iran says it destroyed US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and…

blocks.text: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain – its first direct attack on US military installations for months – in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump announced that he had asked his vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been in the forefront of Republicans saying the war led to the massive Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public, since higher diesel prices was a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

An opinion poll in the UK shows 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was found to be 45%, with 22% opposed.

The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.

Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”

Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.

In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for reviewing Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.

The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.

Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely inside political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.

The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: We tested 6 popular apps to see what data they collect and share. Here’s what we found
articles.summary: Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada — Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube — to find out what data they collect and where it…
articles.byline: Bobby Hristova, Kathleen Coughlin, Rosa Marchitelli

image.caption: Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada – Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, the Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube – to find out what data they collect and where it’s shared. (CBC)

blocks.text: Whether you are buying a coffee, groceries, checking the weather or unwinding with an online video, there’s a free mobile app for just about everything.
But a Marketplace investigation shows the cost of this convenience is your privacy – and the data you’re sharing goes far beyond what you might realize.

Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada — Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, the Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube — to find out what data they collect and where it goes.

To do so, Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science, and his team at the University of Calgary scanned the network traffic of the apps on an Android device. Privo, an organization that evaluates apps to ensure they comply with U.S. child privacy laws, also did a scan of the apps on iOS, Apple’s operating system.

While doing scans to see the network traffic of mobile apps on Android, some apps appeared to be sending information to outside companies around the world. The network scan above shows the activity from all the apps on someone’s phone, not necessarily the apps Marketplace tested. (CBC)
In their user policies, the apps we tested explicitly disclose that they collect or share certain data and that when you use the app, you accept their terms.
But Reardon and Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst who used to work with Privo, are concerned some apps collect more than they need and are sharing what they learn with others around the world.
That data ranges from your name and email address to your exact whereabouts.
“To me, this is not the internet we wanted. This is not the internet we deserve. It's turned into a monstrous data collection surveillance system,” Reardon said.
Here’s what we learned about each app we tested, and what you can do to protect your data.
Tim Hortons
(CBC)
The scan showed that the Tim Hortons app appeared to be sending data to third-party companies as soon as you launch it.

Reardon said one overseas third-party company built into the app appeared to be receiving enough information to create the equivalent of a digital fingerprint for each device, so it can be identified in the future.
“This was beyond the pale,” he said.
Some of those details include:

items: The name given to the device (for example, Bob’s iPhone).
An identifier unique to the device.
A list of many of the sensors on the device.
The details of the device’s camera (for example, the size of your lens).
The names of the ringtones and alarm sounds used.
The names of Wi-Fi routers near you, which Reardon said can be used to determine your location.

blocks.text: Rollason said the third party brands itself as a fraud protection service. She noted the amount of data collected “seems quite excessive” to validate the purchase of a cup of coffee.
Marketplace isn’t identifying any of the third-party companies or their locations because accountability rests with the app developer.

In a statement, Tim Hortons’ director of communications Michael Oliveira said this third party only collects this information for “fraud prevention, account protection, and payment abuse prevention, not for marketing or advertising … or to work around guests’ choices regarding those activities.”
Oliveira said the information collected can help detect if a never-before-seen device is being used on a customer’s account or if a “threat actor” is pretending to be a customer.
He also said the third party is not allowed to sell the data and that Tim Hortons does not sell users’ personal information to third-party companies or data brokers.
PC Optimum

The test showed the PC Optimum app appeared to be sending 10 outside companies information about which products users are searching for — even if the product was sensitive like a search for prenatal vitamins.
One third-party company appeared to be receiving a user’s latitude and longitude and an identifier unique to the device.
The scan also showed the app sending different details to an overseas third-party including:

items: The first name of the user.
Their unredacted email address.
Their PC Optimum member number.
An identifier unique to the device.
How the user interacts with the app, like when they open the app and what they do in the app.

blocks.text: Reardon and Rollason said the data collection seemed to be more than what was necessary for the app to work properly. Based on their experience, they say they didn’t understand why the app needed 10 outside companies to know what users were searching for.
In a statement, Loblaw, the company behind PC Optimum, said the company has never sold personal information and continually reviews and strengthens its systems to protect people.
It said the information collected through Loblaw apps supports everyday features for customers such as shopping online and finding nearby stores.
The Weather Network
The scan showed that when users allowed the Weather Network app access to their location, it appeared to be sending a third-party company those details for targeted advertising, including:

items: A user's precise latitude and longitude.
The user’s local weather conditions.
The device’s advertising ID (unique to each device).

blocks.text: Reardon said it could allow the app to send you advertisements based on where you are or “so you could get ads for a rainy day.”
He also noted it creates a “location history, because all of [the data sent] are bridged by this one thing that doesn't change — this device identifier.”
Rollason said understanding a user’s behaviours is key to advertisers.
“Are you using your phone more when it's raining or you're in the house, perhaps, versus going out on a nice day?” she said.

Pelmorex, the parent company of the Weather Network, said in a statement that the Weather Network does not sell any user data to third parties and data brokers. It said the app only uses location data when a user allows it and uses that data to provide the local weather and show relevant ads. It also said users can access the weather without giving the app their location.
Facebook

The scan showed when users give the Facebook app access to their camera roll to post one image, the app appeared to collect the metadata of other images and videos on the device that were not uploaded.
Metadata contains details like the name of the file, the date and time it was taken and the camera settings.
For whatever image or video is actually posted to Facebook, the scan appeared to show the app also collected the latitude and longitude of where the image was taken.
The app also tracked what users do while using Facebook, including every scroll and how long you linger on something.
Reardon and Rollason noted Facebook didn’t appear to share any data with third-party companies during the scan.

Meta, the parent company of Facebook, had no comment on Marketplace’s findings; however, its privacy policy does state it collects this data. The policy also says “we don't sell any of your information to anyone.”
Amazon
The scan showed Amazon appeared to be collecting what users searched for, even if the product was sensitive, along with the device’s advertising ID.
It didn’t show Amazon sending data to any third-party companies during the scan.
“This is to be expected with these very large companies because they have the resources to have their own ad network,” Reardon said.
Amazon said in a statement it never sells customers’ personal data. It also said it designs products and services to “protect their privacy and to put them in control of their experience."
YouTube
The scan didn’t show YouTube sending data to any third-party companies at the time of the test. The data appeared to only be going to the U.S.
Marketplace also tested if YouTube would follow the rules of its parent company, Google, and not play targeted advertising while a user was watching children’s content.
The test found no targeted ads while watching a children’s video.
Google said in a statement it doesn’t sell personal information.
‘You lack total control’
Ann Cavoukian, the former privacy commissioner of Ontario, said Canada’s current privacy laws aren’t strong enough, and the country's privacy commissioners also need to step up.
Speaking generally, she also said companies should be prioritizing people’s privacy by only collecting what they need and deleting data when they don’t need it anymore.
“You lack total control,” Cavoukian said. “It can be used in a variety of unorganized ways. It can come back to haunt you.”
Ann Cavoukian served as the privacy commissioner of Ontario from 1997 to 2014. (CBC)
The Office of the Federal Privacy Commissioner of Canada declined an interview, but a spokesperson said Marketplace’s findings raise “a number of concerns.”

Speaking generally, the office of Canada’s AI Minister Evan Solomon said in a statement that Canadians need privacy protections that “keep pace with changing technology and the ways companies collect, use and share their data.”

His office also noted the government introduced Bill C-36 to give people more control over their information and to force companies to be more transparent and accountable about how they handle people's data. The bill is still before the House of Commons and has received praise and criticism from privacy experts.
How can you protect your data?
Cavoukian said people should ask companies what data is being collected, why it’s being collected and ask that it be deleted as soon as the company doesn’t need it anymore.

Reardon and Rollason said there’s little you can do to stop the transmission of data because apps on your device, and the third parties in those apps, may be sending or collecting information even when your device is out of reach.
They said deleting apps if you’re not using them and only keeping what you need is the best protection.

articles.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
articles.summary:
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week,…
articles.byline: Ed Walton and Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk

blocks.text: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into a fort near Estoril as Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Zed Jameson/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

articles.title: Nvidia scandal sparks US national security furore and calls to take tough line on China
articles.summary: Former CEO Jensen Huang and US commerce secretary to appear before Congress amid bipartisan concern that America’s security was put at risk

blocks.text: Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy reverberated across the US, sparking bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, who is accused of spying for China.

Donald Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called Jensen Huang two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.

On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Donald Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.

The scandal has also drawn in Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, after criticism of his department’s oversight of Nvidia’s exports to China and its refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.

Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him because: “Recent reports raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.”
Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he did not voluntarily appear. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott said.

Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress after reports emerged of multiple affairs, key among them with Alice Huang, who is no relation but is suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.
House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Jensen Huang’s testimony.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“

Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as the swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for over three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.

Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize
articles.summary:
Political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran, given prestigious Magnitsky humanitarian award

A boxer and political prisoner on death row…

blocks.text: A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.

Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran. He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night.

In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.”
He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’”

blocks.caption: Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’ Photograph: Iran Human Rights

blocks.text: Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK).

He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods.

His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence.

The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption. They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights.

Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.”

blocks.caption: The awards are named after lawyer Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP

blocks.text: According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners.

In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed. In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences.

Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.”

Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.

Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.”

In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”.
He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

articles.title: Teen prodigy, Netflix star, prisoner: the story of Hong Kong dissident Joshua Wong – podcast
articles.summary: Pro-democracy activist Nathan Law and journalist Danny Vincent on the sentencing of the iconic Hong Kong campaigner Joshua Wong to another 10 years in prison.…
articles.byline: Presented by Helen Pidd with Danny Vincent and Nathan Law; produced by Guy Szafman and Brian McNamara; executive producers Sami Kent and Alex Atack

blocks.text: He has been leading protests since he was 14. Joshua Wong has been on the cover of Time magazine, the focus of a Netflix documentary and an icon for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.
Wong has been leading the fight against a Chinese squeeze on freedoms in Hong Kong for the last 15 years. He will now spend more than 16 years in prison.
As Danny Vincent explains, the 30-year-old was sentenced last week to a further 10 years in prison, convicted under the island’s draconian national security law.
Helen Pidd also hears from Joshua’s friend – and fellow movement leader – Nathan Law about the prospects for democracy in Hong Kong.

articles.title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
articles.summary:
Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis

China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of…

blocks.text: China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.

Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year. Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

blocks.caption: A robot shows off its moves at the China Pavilion on the sidelines of Cop31 in Turkey this week. Photograph: Rasit Aydogan/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.

“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said. “They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
after newsletter promotion

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C. That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.

The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand. No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton says ‘Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling’ after Rafah visit
articles.summary:
• F1 driver urges Israel to let aid into Gaza

  • Trip involved tour of facilities with aid workers

Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel…

blocks.text: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel must allow aid ⁠trucks into Gaza, a day after he visited the Rafah border crossing in Egypt.

Hamilton, a seven-time ⁠world champion, arrived ⁠in ​El Arish on Tuesday, where he was briefed on how aid is prepared and coordinated before it ⁠is sent into Gaza, as he toured the Rafah crossing and the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.

He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

“The past ⁠three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an ​injustice for people to ‌be denied their freedom, ‌their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated ‌as though their life matters less,” the Ferrari driver wrote on Instagram.
Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide and says its military campaign in Gaza targets Hamas militants.
Hamilton described seeing food trucks lined up and ready to go at the border that were ‌regularly held up or faced major delays.

“I saw walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in. Standing there, outside what felt like an open-air prison, all I could think about was getting in to help,” he said in the post. “At the Rafah border, I saw food trucks lined up ready to go, but they’re regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours. At the nearby logistics centre, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs even footballs for kids.

“Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. I know so many people feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than just watch. No excuse. I don’t want ⁠us to get used to their suffering. I don’t ​want us to ​look away.”
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.
Hamilton, 41, is an ​advocate for humanitarian causes. In 2021 he founded ​Mission 44, a ‌charity that supports ​young people ​and works to improve their access to education and employment.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine,” Hamilton said last month. “I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage.”
At the crossing on Tuesday, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you”. He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Hamilton is fourth in the drivers’ championship. Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli has won the title with three races to go. The Las Vegas Grand Prix is 21 November before the Qatar Grand Prix on 29 November and the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix on 6 December.

articles.title: Two men found guilty over Iranian attempts to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
articles.summary:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on three people

Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of…

blocks.text: Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of engaging in conduct likely to assist Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Mojtaba Pourmohsen who worked for London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to earn £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.
Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an IRGC commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.
Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”
Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”
Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”
Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”
The pair also discussed surveillance of Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said the Islamic Republic of Iran and its rulers do not and cannot tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.
“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic Republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.
The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.
after newsletter promotion
He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.
Sepahvand claimed his family were being threatened and he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Jonathan Turner of UK Lawyers for Israel.
Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.
Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh ahead of sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
articles.summary:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’

Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has…
articles.byline: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies

blocks.text: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled: “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI,” in which author and journalist Vauhini Vara said AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

Caine prize chair Ellah Wakatama said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations they were using AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: 'We've got to run': Inside ruined Ukraine power plant under constant drone threat
articles.summary: Dan Johnson visits one of the country's largest power stations, barely left standing after a ballistic missile strike by Russia.

blocks.text: As peace talks between Ukraine and Russia continue, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson visits one of the country's power stations on the front lines of the war. Devastated by a direct ballistic missile strike, repair work is hampered by hourly air raids.
Read the BBC's dispatch from Ukraine.
